Appendix contents

Section titles and page numbers link to the corresponding material. Appendix A gives the theory; Appendix B details the experiments of Section 4; Appendix C reports the fixed-choice study and its 32B extension; Appendix E discusses broader impact.

Appendix A Theory and assumptions

This appendix gives the full statements and proofs for repair, comparison, and auditing. For scalar repair, Theorem A.4 identifies information lost through monotone pooling; Theorem A.10 separates score-conditional probe bias from the population probe-loss fitting gap. Theorem A.12 gives observable comparison intervals and the resulting improvement rule; Proposition A.14 gives the directional adoption test used in the main text. Proposition A.17 relates comparison bias to kernel residual moments; Theorems A.20 and A.22 establish the clustered audit and its null test. These results apply established conditional-expectation, projection, model-assisted estimation, and concentration tools under the information and sampling conventions below.

A.1 Notation and definitions: a reader’s guide

The two parts below explain the inputs, prediction target, and repair geometry under the population law used throughout. Appendix A.2 collects the assumptions.

A.1.1 What is the information set, and which loss is used?

The information set is the collection of variables available to a predictor. We represent it by Z=ψ⁡(X,A)Z=\psi(X,A), where XX is a prompt and AA is a generated answer. The base score P=s0​(Z)P=s_{0}(Z) and each candidate s⁡(Z)s(Z) are functions of these inputs. In the shift experiments, ZZ contains the projected final answer state, likelihood summaries and PP; for the archived learned score, Z=(Wψ,P)Z=(W_{\psi},P) contains a learned answer representation and the base score. Reference-free serving excludes the gold reference and correctness label. It does not mean that training or evaluation is label-free, or that ZZ contains all information inside the LLM.

Formally, the information is the σ\sigma-algebra σ⁡(Z)\sigma(Z). With a predictor fixed, two observations sharing ZZ must receive the same score. Previously learned components are held fixed, or conditioned on their independent training data, throughout the population analysis.

The label YY is binary correctness or a grade in [0,1][0,1]. The target m⋆​(Z)=𝔼⁡[Y∣Z]m^{\star}(Z)=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid Z] is therefore a correctness probability or an expected grade. For a confidence value t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1] and predictor ss, define the loss and its population risk by

ℓsq​(Y,t)=(Y−t)2,L⁡(s)=𝔼⁡[ℓsq​(Y,s⁡(Z))].\ell_{\rm sq}(Y,t)=(Y-t)^{2},\qquad L(s)=\mathbb{E}[\ell_{\rm sq}(Y,s(Z))]. (8)

For binary YY, this is the binary Brier convention with one predicted probability. For graded YY, the risk L⁡(s)L(s) is mean-squared error. The squared loss is neither negative log-likelihood nor squared negative log-likelihood: for 0<t<10<t<1, binary log loss is instead −Y​log⁡t−(1−Y)​log⁡(1−t)-Y\log t-(1-Y)\log(1-t). Token-likelihood summaries may be predictor inputs, but they do not change the loss used to evaluate answer correctness.

With repeated answers, ℚ\mathbb{Q} first samples a prompt and then one of its answers uniformly. Thus prompts, not answer rows, receive equal weight in population targets and risks. Equation (9) defines this law when answer counts differ or siblings are dependent.

A.1.2 Miscalibration, monotone projection, and the two remaining losses

The ideal correctness curve for the base score is q⁡(p)=𝔼⁡[Y∣P=p]q(p)=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid P=p], defined up to the score law ν=ℒ⁡(P)\nu=\mathcal{L}(P). Scalar calibration of PP means q⁡(P)=Pq(P)=P almost surely. More generally, a score ss is scalar-calibrated when 𝔼⁡[Y∣s]=s\mathbb{E}[Y\mid s]=s; the stronger condition relative to ZZ is 𝔼⁡[Y−s∣Z]=0\mathbb{E}[Y-s\mid Z]=0. The latter implies the former, but not conversely (Proposition A.2).

A scalar recalibration is a measurable map τ:[0,1]→[0,1]\tau:[0,1]\to[0,1]; its output τ⁡(P)\tau(P) cannot distinguish answers sharing PP. Theorem A.3 separates its risk into outcome noise, score insufficiency, and mapping error:

L⁡(τ⁡(P))=𝔼⁡[Var⁡(Y∣Z)]⏟N+𝔼⁡[Var⁡(m⋆​(Z)∣P)]⏟I+‖τ−q‖L2​(ν)2.L(\tau(P))=\underbrace{\mathbb{E}[\Var(Y\mid Z)]}_{N}+\underbrace{\mathbb{E}[\Var(m^{\star}(Z)\mid P)]}_{I}+\|\tau-q\|_{L^{2}(\nu)}^{2}.

For the unchanged score, the last term is ‖P−q⁡(P)‖22\|P-q(P)\|_{2}^{2}, its squared scalar calibration error. The norm averages under the declared population law; ‖τ−q‖L2​(ν)2=∫(τ⁡(p)−q⁡(p))2​𝑑ν​(p)\|\tau-q\|_{L^{2}(\nu)}^{2}=\int(\tau(p)-q(p))^{2}\,d\nu(p). Insufficiency concerns differences in conditional mean correctness hidden by PP, not merely different realized labels at the same score. The noise term NN is present even for the best predictor using ZZ.

Monotone projection means: among all order-preserving recalibration functions, choose the one closest to the ideal correctness curve in population squared distance. Score values are weighted by their frequency under ν\nu, not uniformly along the horizontal axis of a plot. With ℳ\mathcal{M} the nondecreasing maps [0,1]→[0,1][0,1]\to[0,1], this is

τiso∈arg​minτ∈ℳ∫(τ(p)−q(p))2dν(p),G=∥q−τiso∥L2​(ν)2.\tau_{\rm iso}\in\argmin_{\tau\in\mathcal{M}}\int(\tau(p)-q(p))^{2}\,d\nu(p),\qquad G=\|q-\tau_{\rm iso}\|_{L^{2}(\nu)}^{2}.

Nondecreasing means that score order cannot reverse, although distinct scores may become tied. Pooling combines regions whose ideal correctness values would otherwise violate this order. The population curve qq is unknown; PAIC instead fits to probe predictions, with its target and estimation error analyzed in Appendix A.5.

For the ideal monotone output T=τiso​(P)T=\tau_{\rm iso}(P), the two losses that can remain are:

  • •

    II: differences in expected correctness already hidden by the base score, before recalibration.

  • •

    GG: additional differences lost when the monotone map pools distinct base-score values into the same output.

Theorem A.4 gives

L⁡(T)=N+I+G,𝔼⁡[Y∣T]=T,𝔼⁡[Var⁡(m⋆∣T)]=I+G.L(T)=N+I+G,\qquad\mathbb{E}[Y\mid T]=T,\qquad\mathbb{E}[\Var(m^{\star}\mid T)]=I+G.

Thus I+GI+G is excess risk above L⁡(m⋆)=NL(m^{\star})=N, not residual scalar miscalibration of TT. The components need not both be positive. If ZZ identifies the two families in the introduction, their constant score has N=G=0N=G=0 and I=0.16I=0.16. The three-state example after Theorem A.4 instead has N=I=0N=I=0 and G=1/24G=1/24. The calibration identity is for the ideal population map; a finite PAIC fit need not be scalar-calibrated when probe bias or fitting error remains. For a general non-injective repair, ‖τ−q‖22\|\tau-q\|_{2}^{2} is error relative to the original score’s ideal curve, not necessarily the scalar calibration error of the repaired output itself.

A.2 Information and sampling conventions

The following conditions are used only where indicated.

  1. (T1)

    Let (X,A,Y)(X,A,Y) have a fixed probability law ℚ\mathbb{Q}, where Y∈[0,1]Y\in[0,1] and the spaces are standard Borel. A measurable representation Z=ψ⁡(X,A)Z=\psi(X,A) is fixed. Both s⁡(Z)s(Z) and P=s0​(Z)P=s_{0}(Z) take values in [0,1][0,1] and use this same information. Write ν=ℒ⁡(P)\nu=\mathcal{L}(P) and m⋆​(Z)=𝔼⁡[Y∣Z]m^{\star}(Z)=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid Z]. Conditional expectations and optimal predictors are identified up to equality almost surely. All expectations use the declared population weighting.

  2. (T2)

    For PAIC, let 𝒯n\mathcal{T}_{n} denote standard-Borel training data, independent of nn i.i.d. calibration observations from ℚ\mathbb{Q}. The map (𝒯n,z)↦gn​(z)∈[0,1](\mathcal{T}_{n},z)\mapsto g_{n}(z)\in[0,1] is jointly measurable. For a fresh population observation independent of training, define

    qgn(P)=𝔼[gn(Z)∣P,𝒯n],bn=qgn−q,δn=𝔼train∥bn∥L2​(ν)2.q_{g_{n}}(P)=\mathbb{E}[g_{n}(Z)\mid P,\mathcal{T}_{n}],\qquad b_{n}=q_{g_{n}}-q,\qquad\delta_{n}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathrm{train}}\|b_{n}\|_{L^{2}(\nu)}^{2}.

    The consistency result assumes δn→0\delta_{n}\to 0: probe bias averaged at the base score vanishes. Training randomness is held fixed inside the conditional expectation. Training size may grow with nn. The representation and base score remain fixed; if learned previously, condition on that independent upstream training. This assumption is not a property automatically supplied by a finite probe family. Full probe consistency, 𝔼train​‖gn−m⋆‖22→0\mathbb{E}_{\mathrm{train}}\|g_{n}-m^{\star}\|_{2}^{2}\to 0, is a stronger sufficient condition by conditional-expectation contraction.

  3. (T3)

    For kernel results, kk is a real measurable positive-definite kernel with a separable RKHS ℋk\mathcal{H}_{k}, measurable feature map Φ⁡(z)=k⁡(z,⋅)\Phi(z)=k(z,\cdot), and k⁡(z,z)≤κ<∞k(z,z)\leq\kappa<\infty. Consequently, |k⁡(z,z′)|≤κ|k(z,z^{\prime})|\leq\kappa and ‖Φ⁡(z)‖≤κ\|\Phi(z)\|\leq\sqrt{\kappa}. For the zero-identification theorem, additionally assume that ℋk\mathcal{H}_{k} is dense in L2​(ℚZ)L^{2}(\mathbb{Q}_{Z}). A sufficient condition is that 𝒵\mathcal{Z} is a compact metric space and kk is continuous and universal. This extra condition is not needed for the norm identity or its upper bound.

  4. (T4)

    When prompt-cluster sampling is invoked, comparison or audit data consist of J≥2J\geq 2 i.i.d. prompt clusters Cj=((Zj​i,Yj​i))i=1KjC_{j}=((Z_{ji},Y_{ji}))_{i=1}^{K_{j}}, with 1≤Kj<∞1\leq K_{j}<\infty almost surely. Dependence inside a cluster is unrestricted. All fitted components used in the statistic are fixed independently of these clusters: the probe and entire candidate family for comparisons, or the score and kernel for auditing, including their representation. The population law ℚ\mathbb{Q} is then the prompt-weighted answer law,

    ℚ​f=𝔼C​[1K​∑i=1Kf⁡(Zi,Yi)].\mathbb{Q}f=\mathbb{E}_{C}\left[\frac{1}{K}\sum_{i=1}^{K}f(Z_{i},Y_{i})\right]. (9)

    Cluster results use ℚ\mathbb{Q} for targets, risks, norms, and any kernel-density condition. This equals the usual answer-average weighting when every cluster has the same size; otherwise the two weighting schemes generally define different populations.

Notation.

Set L⁡(s)=𝔼⁡[(Y−s⁡(Z))2]L(s)=\mathbb{E}[(Y-s(Z))^{2}], q⁡(P)=𝔼⁡[Y∣P]q(P)=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid P], N=𝔼⁡[Var⁡(Y∣Z)]N=\mathbb{E}[\Var(Y\mid Z)], and I=𝔼⁡[Var⁡(m⋆​(Z)∣P)]I=\mathbb{E}[\Var(m^{\star}(Z)\mid P)]. The symbol PP denotes the scalar score and ℚ\mathbb{Q} the population law. A composition such as τ∘s0\tau\circ s_{0} is abbreviated by τ⁡(P)\tau(P) inside an expectation. Unless a law is specified, L2L^{2} norms of feature functions use ℚZ\mathbb{Q}_{Z}, and norms of scalar maps use ν\nu. For graded labels, the loss is mean-squared error; the binary case is the Brier score. Results for fixed fitted objects can be read conditionally on their joint training data; independence is required from the subsequent sample on which a comparison or audit is evaluated.

Information use across stages.

Table 2 details the label access and independence conditions behind the workflow in Figure 1. The compact main-text comparison in Table 1 distinguishes the candidates’ fitting targets and serving inputs.

A.3 Population risk and scalar repair limits

Theorem A.1 (Oracle PRCE equals excess squared risk).

Under (T1), every measurable s:𝒵→[0,1]s:\mathcal{Z}\to[0,1] satisfies

L⁡(s)=N+‖s−m⋆‖22,PRCE⁡(s,m⋆)=L⁡(s)−L⁡(m⋆).L(s)=N+\|s-m^{\star}\|_{2}^{2},\qquad\mathrm{PRCE}(s;m^{\star})=L(s)-L(m^{\star}).

Thus m⋆m^{\star} uniquely minimizes risk among ZZ-measurable scores.

Proof.

Insert Y−s=(Y−m⋆)+(m⋆−s)Y-s=(Y-m^{\star})+(m^{\star}-s) into the square. The cross-term is zero because 𝔼⁡[Y−m⋆∣Z]=0\mathbb{E}[Y-m^{\star}\mid Z]=0 and m⋆−sm^{\star}-s is ZZ-measurable. The first squared term is 𝔼⁡[(Y−m⋆)2]=𝔼⁡[Var⁡(Y∣Z)]=N\mathbb{E}[(Y-m^{\star})^{2}]=\mathbb{E}[\Var(Y\mid Z)]=N. The remaining term is ‖s−m⋆‖22\|s-m^{\star}\|_{2}^{2}, which is zero exactly when s=m⋆s=m^{\star} almost surely. ∎

Proposition A.2 (Semantic calibration implies scalar calibration).

Under (T1), s​(Z)=m⋆​(Z)s(Z)=m^{\star}(Z) implies 𝔼⁡[Y∣s⁡(Z)]=s⁡(Z)\mathbb{E}[Y\mid s(Z)]=s(Z). The converse can fail.

Proof.

The tower property gives 𝔼⁡[Y∣s]=𝔼⁡[𝔼⁡[Y∣Z]∣s]=𝔼⁡[s∣s]=s\mathbb{E}[Y\mid s]=\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[Y\mid Z]\mid s]=\mathbb{E}[s\mid s]=s. For the converse, take the two-family population from the introduction: Y=1Y=1 on a family of mass 0.80.8 and Y=0Y=0 on its complement, let ZZ identify the family, and set s=0.8s=0.8. The score is scalar-calibrated but differs from m⋆=Ym^{\star}=Y in both families. ∎

Theorem A.3 (Total-risk decomposition).

Under (T1), for any measurable τ:[0,1]→[0,1]\tau:[0,1]\to[0,1],

L⁡(τ∘s0)=N+I+‖τ−q‖L2​(ν)2.L(\tau\circ s_{0})=N+I+\|\tau-q\|_{L^{2}(\nu)}^{2}. (10)

In particular, PRCE⁡(τ∘s0,m⋆)=I+‖τ−q‖22\mathrm{PRCE}(\tau\circ s_{0};m^{\star})=I+\|\tau-q\|_{2}^{2}. Subtracting the representation-relative optimum L⁡(m⋆)=NL(m^{\star})=N leaves information loss and mapping error.

Proof.

Since P=s0​(Z)P=s_{0}(Z), q⁡(P)=𝔼⁡[m⋆​(Z)∣P]q(P)=\mathbb{E}[m^{\star}(Z)\mid P]. In the squared term of Theorem A.1, write m⋆−τ⁡(P)=(m⋆−q⁡(P))+(q⁡(P)−τ⁡(P))m^{\star}-\tau(P)=(m^{\star}-q(P))+(q(P)-\tau(P)). Its cross-term vanishes after conditioning on PP. The first squared term equals 𝔼⁡[Var⁡(m⋆∣P)]=I\mathbb{E}[\Var(m^{\star}\mid P)]=I; the second is ‖τ−q‖22\|\tau-q\|_{2}^{2}. These are applications of conditional-mean orthogonality underlying classical forecast decompositions (DeGroot and Fienberg, 1983; Bröcker, 2009). The information term also exposes the within-score heterogeneity studied as grouping loss (Perez-Lebel et al., 2023). ∎

Restricting the repair class.

Let

ℳ={τ:[0,1]→[0,1]:τ is nondecreasing}\mathcal{M}=\{\tau:[0,1]\to[0,1]:\tau\text{ is nondecreasing}\}

be the set of actual bounded nondecreasing maps; these maps are Borel measurable. Write [τ]ν[\tau]_{\nu} for the equivalence class modulo ν\nu-almost-everywhere equality, and define its quotient image

ℳ¯={[τ]ν:τ∈ℳ}⊂L2​(ν).\overline{\mathcal{M}}=\{[\tau]_{\nu}:\tau\in\mathcal{M}\}\subset L^{2}(\nu).

Empirical objectives are evaluated on maps in ℳ\mathcal{M}, including their values at observed scores. Population projection takes place in ℳ¯\overline{\mathcal{M}}. Choosing actual representatives specifies values at observed scores and keeps empirical fitting distinct from population uniqueness modulo ν\nu.

Theorem A.4 (Monotone projection and the remaining gap).

The set ℳ¯\overline{\mathcal{M}} is nonempty, closed, and convex. The projection of [q]ν[q]_{\nu} onto it is a unique class [τiso]ν[\tau_{\mathrm{iso}}]_{\nu}. Choose and fix a representative τiso∈ℳ\tau_{\mathrm{iso}}\in\mathcal{M} of this class. With G=‖q−τiso‖22G=\|q-\tau_{\mathrm{iso}}\|_{2}^{2},

infτ∈ℳL⁡(τ∘s0)\displaystyle\inf_{\tau\in\mathcal{M}}L(\tau\circ s_{0}) =N+I+G,\displaystyle=N+I+G, (11)
‖τ−τiso‖22\displaystyle\|\tau-\tau_{\mathrm{iso}}\|_{2}^{2} ≤∥τ−q∥22−G(τ∈ℳ).\displaystyle\leq\|\tau-q\|_{2}^{2}-G\quad(\tau\in\mathcal{M}). (12)

The gap GG is zero if and only if qq has a nondecreasing version. The maximal improvement over the unchanged score is ‖id−q‖22−G≥0\|\mathrm{id}-q\|_{2}^{2}-G\geq 0, since the identity map belongs to ℳ\mathcal{M}. Moreover, for T=τiso​(P)T=\tau_{\mathrm{iso}}(P),

𝔼⁡[Y∣T]=T,𝔼⁡[Var⁡(m⋆​(Z)∣T)]=I+G.\mathbb{E}[Y\mid T]=T,\qquad\mathbb{E}[\Var(m^{\star}(Z)\mid T)]=I+G. (13)

Thus GG is additional output grouping loss, even though the projected score is scalar-calibrated.

Proof.

Constants belong to ℳ\mathcal{M}, and convex combinations preserve bounds and order, so ℳ¯\overline{\mathcal{M}} is nonempty and convex. For closedness, take an L2​(ν)L^{2}(\nu)-convergent sequence in ℳ¯\overline{\mathcal{M}}, choose representatives in ℳ\mathcal{M}, and extract an almost-everywhere convergent subsequence. Its pointwise limit on a full-measure set is bounded and nondecreasing there, and extends monotonically to [0,1][0,1]. Values at atoms are retained; right-continuity is not imposed. The limit class therefore belongs to ℳ¯\overline{\mathcal{M}}. The Hilbert-space projection theorem on this closed convex set gives existence, uniqueness modulo ν\nu, and ⟨q−τiso,τ−τiso⟩≤0\langle q-\tau_{\mathrm{iso}},\tau-\tau_{\mathrm{iso}}\rangle\leq 0. Expanding ‖τ−q‖22\|\tau-q\|_{2}^{2} proves (12); combining with Theorem A.3 proves the optimum and improvement formula. Closedness gives the characterization of G=0G=0.

To establish output calibration without a continuity assumption on ν\nu, write T=τiso​(P)T=\tau_{\mathrm{iso}}(P) and R=q⁡(P)−TR=q(P)-T. For any Lipschitz function hh compactly supported in (0,1)(0,1), the maps v↦v±ϵ​h​(v)v\mapsto v\pm\epsilon h(v) are nondecreasing and remain in [0,1][0,1] for sufficiently small ϵ>0\epsilon>0. Composing them with τiso\tau_{\mathrm{iso}} gives feasible perturbations in both directions. The projection inequality implies 𝔼⁡[R​h​(T)]=0\mathbb{E}[Rh(T)]=0. Such functions determine the finite signed residual measure on (0,1)(0,1), so 𝔼⁡[R∣T]=0\mathbb{E}[R\mid T]=0 on that interval, including its atoms.

For the endpoints, use the feasible maps max⁡(T,a)\max(T,a) and min⁡(T,1−a)\min(T,1-a). Divide their variational inequalities by a>0a>0 and let a↓0a\downarrow 0. Dominated convergence gives

𝔼[q(P)𝟏{T=0}]≤0,𝔼[(1−q(P))𝟏{T=1}]≤0.\mathbb{E}[q(P)\mathbf{1}\{T=0\}]\leq 0,\qquad\mathbb{E}[(1-q(P))\mathbf{1}\{T=1\}]\leq 0.

Both integrands are nonnegative; hence both expectations vanish. It follows that 𝔼⁡[q⁡(P)∣T]=T\mathbb{E}[q(P)\mid T]=T everywhere almost surely, and the tower property gives 𝔼⁡[Y∣T]=𝔼⁡[m⋆∣T]=T\mathbb{E}[Y\mid T]=\mathbb{E}[m^{\star}\mid T]=T. Finally, conditional-mean orthogonality yields

𝔼⁡[Var⁡(m⋆∣T)]=𝔼⁡[(m⋆−T)2]=𝔼⁡[(m⋆−q⁡(P))2]+𝔼⁡[(q⁡(P)−T)2]=I+G.\mathbb{E}[\Var(m^{\star}\mid T)]=\mathbb{E}[(m^{\star}-T)^{2}]=\mathbb{E}[(m^{\star}-q(P))^{2}]+\mathbb{E}[(q(P)-T)^{2}]=I+G.

This connects isotonic pooling to standard calibration and grouping-loss decompositions (Dimitriadis et al., 2021; Perez-Lebel et al., 2023). ∎

Information and ordering are distinct.

Put equal mass on three states with P=(0,1/2,1)P=(0,1/2,1) and Y=m⋆=q=(0,1,1/2)Y=m^{\star}=q=(0,1,1/2). Spearman correlation is 1/2>01/2>0, but qq is not nondecreasing. Its isotonic projection is (0,3/4,3/4)(0,3/4,3/4), so I=0I=0 and G=1/24>0G=1/24>0. The score retains all predictive information here; only the monotonicity restriction prevents perfect prediction.

Information versus learnability.

The term II uses all measurable scalar predictors. For a restricted class 𝒜\mathcal{A} of scalar maps, the best risk is instead N+I+infτ∈𝒜‖τ−q‖22N+I+\inf_{\tau\in\mathcal{A}}\|\tau-q\|_{2}^{2}, before estimation or optimization error. On a finite or countable full-measure state set, an injective score can retain all information in ZZ, giving I=0I=0, even when learning a useful restricted remapping is difficult. Better performance by a fitted feature-dependent predictor therefore need not establish I>0I>0.

A.4 Probe-based comparisons of candidate repairs

A probe supplies a fitted comparison target. We first separate its error from oracle excess risk, then compare two scores directly. The paired calculation cancels terms shared by the candidates and is therefore more informative for a repair decision than two separate absolute-error bounds.

For fixed scores ss and gg under the same population law, define Probe-Relative Calibration Error by

PRCE⁡(s,g)=𝔼⁡[(s⁡(Z)−g⁡(Z))2].\mathrm{PRCE}(s;g)=\mathbb{E}[(s(Z)-g(Z))^{2}].

This measures squared disagreement with gg. The oracle identity PRCE⁡(s,m⋆)=L⁡(s)−L⁡(m⋆)\mathrm{PRCE}(s;m^{\star})=L(s)-L(m^{\star}) follows from Theorem A.1.

Theorem A.5 (Fixed-probe discrepancy and oracle excess risk).

Under (T1), for fixed s,g:𝒵→[0,1]s,g:\mathcal{Z}\to[0,1], let e=g−m⋆e=g-m^{\star}. Then

PRCE⁡(s,g)−PRCE⁡(s,m⋆)\displaystyle\mathrm{PRCE}(s;g)-\mathrm{PRCE}(s;m^{\star}) =‖e‖22−2​𝔼​[(s−m⋆)​e],\displaystyle=\|e\|_{2}^{2}-2\mathbb{E}[(s-m^{\star})e], (14)
|PRCE⁡(s,g)−PRCE⁡(s,m⋆)|\displaystyle\left|\mathrm{PRCE}(s;g)-\mathrm{PRCE}(s;m^{\star})\right| ≤2​𝔼​|e|≤2​‖e‖2.\displaystyle\leq 2\mathbb{E}|e|\leq 2\|e\|_{2}. (15)

An independent evaluation average is unbiased for PRCE⁡(s,g)\mathrm{PRCE}(s;g), conditional on the fitted ss and gg.

Proof.

Expand (s−g)2=(s−m⋆−e)2(s-g)^{2}=(s-m^{\star}-e)^{2} for the first identity. For the bound, factor the difference of squares: |(s−g)2−(s−m⋆)2|=|e|​|g+m⋆−2​s|≤2​|e||(s-g)^{2}-(s-m^{\star})^{2}|=|e|\,|g+m^{\star}-2s|\leq 2|e|. Cauchy–Schwarz bounds its expectation. Unbiasedness for the fixed-probe quantity follows by taking the expectation of each independently evaluated summand. Equal-prompt averages have the same property under (9). This statement concerns a fixed candidate; selection on the comparison sample requires simultaneous control, given below. ∎

Proposition A.6 (Pairwise transfer from probe agreement to risk).

Under (T1), fix sa,sb,g:𝒵→[0,1]s_{a},s_{b},g:\mathcal{Z}\to[0,1]. Write Dg​(a,b)=PRCE⁡(sa,g)−PRCE⁡(sb,g)D_{g}(a,b)=\mathrm{PRCE}(s_{a};g)-\mathrm{PRCE}(s_{b};g) and Δa​b=L⁡(sa)−L⁡(sb)\Delta_{ab}=L(s_{a})-L(s_{b}). Then

Dg​(a,b)−Δa​b\displaystyle D_{g}(a,b)-\Delta_{ab} =−2​𝔼​[(sa−sb)​(g−m⋆)],\displaystyle=-2\mathbb{E}[(s_{a}-s_{b})(g-m^{\star})], (16)
|Dg​(a,b)−Δa​b|\displaystyle|D_{g}(a,b)-\Delta_{ab}| ≤2​‖sa−sb‖2​‖g−m⋆‖2.\displaystyle\leq 2\|s_{a}-s_{b}\|_{2}\|g-m^{\star}\|_{2}. (17)

In particular, if ρg≥‖g−m⋆‖2\rho_{g}\geq\|g-m^{\star}\|_{2} and Dg​(a,b)<−2​ρg​‖sa−sb‖2D_{g}(a,b)<-2\rho_{g}\|s_{a}-s_{b}\|_{2}, then L⁡(sa)<L⁡(sb)L(s_{a})<L(s_{b}). For scalar candidates sa=τa​(P)s_{a}=\tau_{a}(P) and sb=τb​(P)s_{b}=\tau_{b}(P), let bg​(P)=𝔼⁡[g⁡(Z)−Y∣P]b_{g}(P)=\mathbb{E}[g(Z)-Y\mid P]. The sharper identity and bound are

Dg​(a,b)−Δa​b=−2​⟨τa−τb,bg⟩L2​(ν),|Dg​(a,b)−Δa​b|≤2​‖τa−τb‖2​‖bg‖2.D_{g}(a,b)-\Delta_{ab}=-2\langle\tau_{a}-\tau_{b},b_{g}\rangle_{L^{2}(\nu)},\qquad|D_{g}(a,b)-\Delta_{ab}|\leq 2\|\tau_{a}-\tau_{b}\|_{2}\|b_{g}\|_{2}. (18)
Proof.

Subtract the expansions in Theorem A.5 for aa and bb. The shared term ‖g−m⋆‖22\|g-m^{\star}\|_{2}^{2} cancels, while Theorem A.1 gives PRCE⁡(sa,m⋆)−PRCE⁡(sb,m⋆)=Δa​b\mathrm{PRCE}(s_{a};m^{\star})-\mathrm{PRCE}(s_{b};m^{\star})=\Delta_{ab}. This proves (16). Cauchy–Schwarz gives (17); the strict margin then implies Δa​b≤Dg​(a,b)+2​ρg​‖sa−sb‖2<0\Delta_{ab}\leq D_{g}(a,b)+2\rho_{g}\|s_{a}-s_{b}\|_{2}<0. For scalar candidates, condition the product in (16) on PP and use 𝔼⁡[g−m⋆∣P]=𝔼⁡[g−Y∣P]=bg\mathbb{E}[g-m^{\star}\mid P]=\mathbb{E}[g-Y\mid P]=b_{g}. ∎

The identity isolates the direction of probe error relevant to a comparison. If g−m⋆g-m^{\star} is orthogonal to sa−sbs_{a}-s_{b}, the two differences agree even when the probe is imperfect. Otherwise their signs can differ. This is a population statement about squared correctness risk, with a common target and law for both candidates.

Corollary A.7 (Uncorrected comparisons: a bias-dependent benchmark).

Under (T1) and the cluster sampling in (T4), condition on a jointly fitted probe gg and M≥2M\geq 2 candidates s1,…,sMs_{1},\ldots,s_{M}, all frozen independently of the JJ comparison clusters. All population quantities in this corollary use ℚ\mathbb{Q}, including m⋆=𝔼ℚ​[Y∣Z]m^{\star}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{Q}}[Y\mid Z]. Define

R^cg=1J​∑j=1J1Kj​∑i=1Kj(sc​(Zj​i)−g⁡(Zj​i))2,D^a​b=R^ag−R^bg.\widehat{R}_{c}^{g}=\frac{1}{J}\sum_{j=1}^{J}\frac{1}{K_{j}}\sum_{i=1}^{K_{j}}(s_{c}(Z_{ji})-g(Z_{ji}))^{2},\qquad\widehat{D}_{ab}=\widehat{R}_{a}^{g}-\widehat{R}_{b}^{g}.

Write eg=‖g−m⋆‖2e_{g}=\|g-m^{\star}\|_{2} and da​b=‖sa−sb‖2d_{ab}=\|s_{a}-s_{b}\|_{2}. For 0<α<10<\alpha<1, set tJ,M,α=(2/J)​log⁡(M⁡(M−1)/α)t_{J,M,\alpha}=\sqrt{(2/J)\log(M(M-1)/\alpha)}. With conditional probability at least 1−α1-\alpha, simultaneously for every pair,

|D^a​b−[L⁡(sa)−L⁡(sb)]|≤2​eg​da​b+tJ,M,α≤2​eg+tJ,M,α.|\widehat{D}_{ab}-[L(s_{a})-L(s_{b})]|\leq 2e_{g}d_{ab}+t_{J,M,\alpha}\leq 2e_{g}+t_{J,M,\alpha}. (19)

On the same event, any measurable empirical minimizer c^∈arg​min1≤c≤M⁡R^cg\hat{c}\in\argmin_{1\leq c\leq M}\widehat{R}_{c}^{g} satisfies

L⁡(sc^)−min1≤c≤M⁡L⁡(sc)≤2​eg+tJ,M,α.L(s_{\hat{c}})-\min_{1\leq c\leq M}L(s_{c})\leq 2e_{g}+t_{J,M,\alpha}. (20)
Proof.

For each pair, the within-prompt average of squared-loss differences lies in [−1,1][-1,1], has expectation Dg​(a,b)D_{g}(a,b), and is independent across prompts. Hoeffding’s inequality (Hoeffding, 1963) gives

Pr{|D^a​b−Dg(a,b)|>t}≤2exp(−Jt2/2).\Pr\{|\widehat{D}_{ab}-D_{g}(a,b)|>t\}\leq 2\exp(-Jt^{2}/2).

There are M⁡(M−1)/2M(M-1)/2 unordered pairs; reversing a pair only changes its sign. A union bound with the displayed tJ,M,αt_{J,M,\alpha} and Proposition A.6 proves (19). Since bounded scores give da​b≤1d_{ab}\leq 1, the second inequality follows. If c⋆c^{\star} minimizes true risk within the family, empirical optimality gives D^c^​c⋆≤0\widehat{D}_{\hat{c}c^{\star}}\leq 0. Apply the simultaneous event to this selected pair to obtain (20). Bounded cluster averages require no moment assumption on the finite cluster sizes. ∎

Interpreting a conditional comparison bound.

The corollary allows selection within the frozen family; fitting or tuning candidates on these comparison prompts requires additional control, even if their labels are unused. The probe error ege_{g} remains unknown. For example, an honest upper confidence bound Ug≥L⁡(g)U_{g}\geq L(g) from labeled validation under the same law supplies eg2=L⁡(g)−N≤Uge_{g}^{2}=L(g)-N\leq U_{g}. If this bound has coverage 1−β1-\beta, using Ug\sqrt{U_{g}} in place of ege_{g} gives joint coverage at least 1−α−β1-\alpha-\beta by a union bound. The radius is conservative because labeled probe risk retains outcome noise. Thus the result states the ingredients needed for a reliable surrogate comparison; it neither estimates probe accuracy from unlabeled agreement nor demonstrates a selection advantage over ordinary labeled validation.

A.5 PAIC: fixed-probe target and empirical consistency

Before studying increasing training and calibration samples, consider the population repair obtained from one fixed probe. This separates error in the anchor from error in fitting a monotone curve to finitely many examples.

Proposition A.8 (Fixed-probe projection and additional risk).

Under (T1), fix g:𝒵→[0,1]g:\mathcal{Z}\to[0,1] and let qg​(P)=𝔼⁡[g⁡(Z)∣P]q_{g}(P)=\mathbb{E}[g(Z)\mid P]. Choose a representative τg∈ℳ\tau_{g}\in\mathcal{M} of the projection of qgq_{g} onto ℳ¯\overline{\mathcal{M}}. This is also the unique population minimizing class for 𝔼⁡[(g⁡(Z)−τ⁡(P))2]\mathbb{E}[(g(Z)-\tau(P))^{2}]. Then

‖τg−τiso‖L2​(ν)\displaystyle\|\tau_{g}-\tau_{\mathrm{iso}}\|_{L^{2}(\nu)} ≤‖qg−q‖L2​(ν)≤‖g−m⋆‖2,\displaystyle\leq\|q_{g}-q\|_{L^{2}(\nu)}\leq\|g-m^{\star}\|_{2}, (21)
0≤L⁡(τg∘s0)−(N+I+G)\displaystyle 0\leq L(\tau_{g}\circ s_{0})-(N+I+G) ≤‖qg−q‖L2​(ν)2≤‖g−m⋆‖22.\displaystyle\leq\|q_{g}-q\|_{L^{2}(\nu)}^{2}\leq\|g-m^{\star}\|_{2}^{2}. (22)

For Tg=τg​(P)T_{g}=\tau_{g}(P), 𝔼⁡[g∣Tg]=Tg\mathbb{E}[g\mid T_{g}]=T_{g}, while

𝔼⁡[Y∣Tg]−Tg=𝔼⁡[m⋆−g∣Tg].\mathbb{E}[Y\mid T_{g}]-T_{g}=\mathbb{E}[m^{\star}-g\mid T_{g}]. (23)
Proof.

Conditioning on PP gives 𝔼⁡[(g−τ⁡(P))2]=𝔼⁡[Var⁡(g∣P)]+‖qg−τ‖22\mathbb{E}[(g-\tau(P))^{2}]=\mathbb{E}[\Var(g\mid P)]+\|q_{g}-\tau\|_{2}^{2}, so the minimizing class is the projection of qgq_{g}. Write d=τg−τisod=\tau_{g}-\tau_{\mathrm{iso}} and h=qg−qh=q_{g}-q as elements of L2​(ν)L^{2}(\nu). Adding the variational inequalities for the two projections gives ‖d‖22≤⟨d,h⟩\|d\|_{2}^{2}\leq\langle d,h\rangle and hence ‖d‖2≤‖h‖2\|d\|_{2}\leq\|h\|_{2}. Conditional-expectation contraction gives ‖h‖2=‖𝔼⁡[g−m⋆∣P]‖2≤‖g−m⋆‖2\|h\|_{2}=\|\mathbb{E}[g-m^{\star}\mid P]\|_{2}\leq\|g-m^{\star}\|_{2}.

Apply the projection inequality with target qgq_{g} and competitor τiso\tau_{\mathrm{iso}} to obtain ‖τg−qg‖22−‖τiso−qg‖22≤−‖d‖22\|\tau_{g}-q_{g}\|_{2}^{2}-\|\tau_{\mathrm{iso}}-q_{g}\|_{2}^{2}\leq-\|d\|_{2}^{2}. By Theorem A.3,

L⁡(τg∘s0)−L⁡(τiso∘s0)\displaystyle L(\tau_{g}\circ s_{0})-L(\tau_{\mathrm{iso}}\circ s_{0}) =‖τg−q‖22−‖τiso−q‖22\displaystyle=\|\tau_{g}-q\|_{2}^{2}-\|\tau_{\mathrm{iso}}-q\|_{2}^{2}
≤2​⟨d,h⟩−‖d‖22=‖h‖22−‖h−d‖22≤‖h‖22.\displaystyle\leq 2\langle d,h\rangle-\|d\|_{2}^{2}=\|h\|_{2}^{2}-\|h-d\|_{2}^{2}\leq\|h\|_{2}^{2}.

The lower bound follows from optimality of τiso\tau_{\mathrm{iso}}. Apply the output-calibration argument of Theorem A.4 with gg in place of YY to obtain 𝔼⁡[g∣Tg]=Tg\mathbb{E}[g\mid T_{g}]=T_{g}. Subtract this identity from 𝔼⁡[Y∣Tg]=𝔼⁡[m⋆∣Tg]\mathbb{E}[Y\mid T_{g}]=\mathbb{E}[m^{\star}\mid T_{g}] for (23). ∎

Consequently, the fixed-probe population repair improves on the base score whenever ‖id−q‖22−G>‖qg−q‖22\|\mathrm{id}-q\|_{2}^{2}-G>\|q_{g}-q\|_{2}^{2}: the available monotone gain then exceeds the bound on anchor error. This is a sufficient population condition. A fitted finite-sample repair also incurs calibration error, addressed next.

Measurable population and empirical maps.

A regular conditional kernel KZ​(p,d​z)K_{Z}(p,dz) gives the jointly measurable version qg​(t,p)=∫g⁡(t,z)​KZ​(p,𝑑z)q_{g}(t,p)=\int g(t,z)K_{Z}(p,dz). The space L2​(ν)L^{2}(\nu) is separable and projection onto ℳ¯\overline{\mathcal{M}} is continuous, so the projected class is measurable in training data. One jointly measurable monotone representative of a projected class ff is its prefix essential supremum, equivalently

f♯​(p)=sup({0}∪{r∈ℚ∩[0,1]:∫[0,p](f⁡(u)−r)+​𝑑ν​(u)>0}).f^{\sharp}(p)=\sup\left(\{0\}\cup\left\{r\in\mathbb{Q}\cap[0,1]:\int_{[0,p]}(f(u)-r)_{+}\,d\nu(u)>0\right\}\right).

The integrals depend only on the class and are jointly measurable in the class and pp. For a monotone class this representative agrees ν\nu-almost everywhere and retains every atom; empty prefixes take value zero. Empirical minimizers, in contrast, retain their actual observed values. Stable sorting, pooling tied scores, and a specified monotone interpolation give a jointly measurable empirical map.

Lemma A.9 (Uniform loss deviation for an independently fitted anchor).

Let ℚn\mathbb{Q}_{n} be the empirical measure of nn i.i.d. calibration observations under (T1). For each fixed measurable g:𝒵→[0,1]g:\mathcal{Z}\to[0,1], there is a bounded measurable Δn​(g)\Delta_{n}(g) with

supa∈ℳ|(ℚn−ℚ)​(a⁡(P)−g⁡(Z))2|≤Δn​(g),𝔼cal​Δn​(g)≤C0n,C0=252.\sup_{a\in\mathcal{M}}\left|(\mathbb{Q}_{n}-\mathbb{Q})(a(P)-g(Z))^{2}\right|\leq\Delta_{n}(g),\qquad\mathbb{E}_{\rm cal}\Delta_{n}(g)\leq\frac{C_{0}}{\sqrt{n}},\quad C_{0}=\frac{25}{2}.

The constant is uniform over fixed bounded anchors and all score laws, including laws with atoms. The statement therefore applies conditionally to the independent, possibly changing gng_{n} in (T2).

Proof.

Let ℋ↑\mathcal{H}_{\uparrow} contain the open and closed upper half-lines in [0,1][0,1], including the empty and full sets. For fixed measurable 0≤w⁡(Z)≤10\leq w(Z)\leq 1, define

Dn(w)=supH∈ℋ↑|(ℚn−ℚ)w(Z)𝟏{P∈H}|.D_{n}(w)=\sup_{H\in\mathcal{H}_{\uparrow}}|(\mathbb{Q}_{n}-\mathbb{Q})w(Z)\mathbf{1}\{P\in H\}|.

One-sided limits of rational cuts recover open and closed half-lines, so the supremum is measurable. Symmetrization with independent Rademacher signs εi\varepsilon_{i} and decreasing-score ordering gives

𝔼​Dn​(w)≤2n​𝔼​max0≤l≤n​|∑i=1lε(i)​w​(Z(i))|≤4n.\mathbb{E}D_{n}(w)\leq\frac{2}{n}\mathbb{E}\max_{0\leq l\leq n}\left|\sum_{i=1}^{l}\varepsilon_{(i)}w(Z_{(i)})\right|\leq\frac{4}{\sqrt{n}}.

For the last inequality, condition on the observations. The weighted partial sums form a martingale, and Doob’s L2L^{2} maximal inequality bounds their expected maximum by 2​(∑iw​(Zi)2)1/2≤2​n2(\sum_{i}w(Z_{i})^{2})^{1/2}\leq 2\sqrt{n}. Ties only reduce the attainable prefixes. For any bounded nondecreasing aa, every superlevel set {p:a⁡(p)>u}\{p:a(p)>u\} is such a half-line. The layer-cake identities

a(p)2=∫012u 1{a(p)>u}du,a(p)=∫01𝟏{a(p)>u}dua(p)^{2}=\int_{0}^{1}2u\,\mathbf{1}\{a(p)>u\}\,du,\qquad a(p)=\int_{0}^{1}\mathbf{1}\{a(p)>u\}\,du

imply a uniform bound with

Δn​(g)=Dn​(1)+2​Dn​(g)+|(ℚn−ℚ)​g2|.\Delta_{n}(g)=D_{n}(1)+2D_{n}(g)+|(\mathbb{Q}_{n}-\mathbb{Q})g^{2}|.

The final term has expectation at most 1/(2​n)1/(2\sqrt{n}) because g2∈[0,1]g^{2}\in[0,1]. Adding the bounds gives C0=25/2C_{0}=25/2. Uniformity is over monotone maps for each fixed anchor, not over anchors chosen using the calibration observations. Training independence allows conditioning on gng_{n} before applying the bound. ∎

Theorem A.10 (PAIC risk and consistency under score-conditional bias).

Under (T1) and (T2), let τ^n∈ℳ\hat{\tau}_{n}\in\mathcal{M} be a jointly measurable empirical minimizer of n−1​∑i(τ⁡(Pi)−gn​(Zi))2n^{-1}\sum_{i}(\tau(P_{i})-g_{n}(Z_{i}))^{2} over actual maps τ∈ℳ\tau\in\mathcal{M}. Let τgn\tau_{g_{n}} be the population projection of qgnq_{g_{n}}, and define, conditionally on training,

Rgn​(a)=ℚ​(gn​(Z)−a⁡(P))2,un=Rgn​(τ^n)−Rgn​(τgn)≥0.R_{g_{n}}(a)=\mathbb{Q}(g_{n}(Z)-a(P))^{2},\qquad u_{n}=R_{g_{n}}(\hat{\tau}_{n})-R_{g_{n}}(\tau_{g_{n}})\geq 0.

Then almost surely

‖τ^n−τiso‖22≤L⁡(τ^n∘s0)−(N+I+G)≤(‖bn‖2+un)2,un≤2​Δn​(gn).\|\hat{\tau}_{n}-\tau_{\mathrm{iso}}\|_{2}^{2}\leq L(\hat{\tau}_{n}\circ s_{0})-(N+I+G)\leq(\|b_{n}\|_{2}+\sqrt{u_{n}})^{2},\qquad u_{n}\leq 2\Delta_{n}(g_{n}). (24)

In particular,

𝔼train,cal​[L⁡(τ^n∘s0)−(N+I+G)]≤(δn+2​C0n)2≤2​δn+4​C0n.\mathbb{E}_{\mathrm{train,cal}}\big[L(\hat{\tau}_{n}\circ s_{0})-(N+I+G)\big]\leq\left(\sqrt{\delta_{n}}+\sqrt{\frac{2C_{0}}{\sqrt{n}}}\right)^{2}\leq 2\delta_{n}+\frac{4C_{0}}{\sqrt{n}}. (25)

Thus δn→0\delta_{n}\to 0 implies risk convergence to N+I+GN+I+G and squared L2​(ν)L^{2}(\nu) convergence of the map to τiso\tau_{\mathrm{iso}}, both in mean and in probability. The rate is a non-sharp uniform consistency bound, not an observable confidence interval or a guarantee at ν\nu-null scores.

Proof.

Condition on training. Empirical optimality and Lemma A.9 imply un≤2​Δn​(gn)u_{n}\leq 2\Delta_{n}(g_{n}). Write d=τgn−τisod=\tau_{g_{n}}-\tau_{\mathrm{iso}}, e=τ^n−τgne=\hat{\tau}_{n}-\tau_{g_{n}}, and b=bnb=b_{n}. Projection at target qgnq_{g_{n}} gives

‖e‖22≤un,Rgn​(τgn)−Rgn​(τiso)≤−‖d‖22.\|e\|_{2}^{2}\leq u_{n},\qquad R_{g_{n}}(\tau_{g_{n}})-R_{g_{n}}(\tau_{\mathrm{iso}})\leq-\|d\|_{2}^{2}.

Differences of label risks equal differences of probe risks plus 2​⟨map difference,b⟩2\langle\text{map difference},b\rangle. Therefore

L⁡(τ^n∘s0)−L⁡(τiso∘s0)\displaystyle L(\hat{\tau}_{n}\circ s_{0})-L(\tau_{\mathrm{iso}}\circ s_{0}) ≤un−‖d‖22+2​⟨d+e,b⟩\displaystyle\leq u_{n}-\|d\|_{2}^{2}+2\langle d+e,b\rangle
=un+‖b‖22−‖d−b‖22+2​⟨e,b⟩\displaystyle=u_{n}+\|b\|_{2}^{2}-\|d-b\|_{2}^{2}+2\langle e,b\rangle
≤(un+‖b‖2)2.\displaystyle\leq(\sqrt{u_{n}}+\|b\|_{2})^{2}.

Projection at the true target qq gives the lower inequality in (24). Taking expectations, using 𝔼​un≤2​C0/n\mathbb{E}u_{n}\leq 2C_{0}/\sqrt{n} and Cauchy–Schwarz on 𝔼⁡[‖bn‖2​un]\mathbb{E}[\|b_{n}\|_{2}\sqrt{u_{n}}] proves (25). Markov’s inequality gives convergence in probability. This argument uses projection inequalities rather than linearity of the projection. ∎

Sharper fitting rate and scalar-calibration minimax order.

Condition on probe training and write ℓa=(a⁡(P)−gn​(Z))2\ell_{a}=(a(P)-g_{n}(Z))^{2}. The loss differences fa=ℓa−ℓτgnf_{a}=\ell_{a}-\ell_{\tau_{g_{n}}}, a∈ℳa\in\mathcal{M}, satisfy 𝔼​fa2≤4​‖a−τgn‖22≤4​𝔼​fa\mathbb{E}f_{a}^{2}\leq 4\|a-\tau_{g_{n}}\|_{2}^{2}\leq 4\mathbb{E}f_{a}: squared loss is 22-Lipschitz on [0,1][0,1], and projection at qgnq_{g_{n}} gives the second inequality. The monotone class has L2​(μ)L^{2}(\mu) bracketing entropy of order 1/η1/\eta uniformly over probability measures μ\mu (van der Vaart and Wellner, 1996, Thm. 2.7.5, p. 159). For the loss differences with 𝔼​fa2≤r\mathbb{E}f_{a}^{2}\leq r, chaining bounds the expected local Rademacher complexity by a constant times n−1/2r1/4+n−2/3n^{-1/2}r^{1/4}+n^{-2/3}. This sub-root bound has fixed point of order n−2/3n^{-2/3}; Bartlett et al. (2005, Thm. 3.3(1)) therefore gives 𝔼[un∣𝒯n]≤Cn−2/3\mathbb{E}[u_{n}\mid\mathcal{T}_{n}]\leq Cn^{-2/3} for a universal CC, without requiring qq or qgnq_{g_{n}} to be monotone. Related fixed-design bounds for error relative to the monotone projection under misspecification are given by Chatterjee et al. (2015, Thm. 6.1); here localization controls the full excess probe loss unu_{n}. Theorem A.10 therefore gives

𝔼L(τ^n∘s0)−(N+I+G)≤(δn+Cn−1/3)2.\mathbb{E}L(\hat{\tau}_{n}\circ s_{0})-(N+I+G)\leq\bigl(\sqrt{\delta_{n}}+\sqrt{C}\,n^{-1/3}\bigr)^{2}.

For i.i.d. prompt clusters, put Fa​(C)=K−1​∑ifa​(Zi)F_{a}(C)=K^{-1}\sum_{i}f_{a}(Z_{i}). Jensen gives 𝔼​Fa2≤4​‖a−τgn‖22≤4​𝔼​Fa\mathbb{E}F_{a}^{2}\leq 4\|a-\tau_{g_{n}}\|_{2}^{2}\leq 4\mathbb{E}F_{a} and ‖Fa−Fb‖L2​(ℚJ)≤2​‖a−b‖L2​(μJ)\|F_{a}-F_{b}\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{Q}_{J})}\leq 2\|a-b\|_{L^{2}(\mu_{J})}, where μJ=J−1​∑jKj−1​∑iδPj​i\mu_{J}=J^{-1}\sum_{j}K_{j}^{-1}\sum_{i}\delta_{P_{ji}} is a probability measure. Thus the same entropy argument applies with JJ in place of nn, under the prompt-weighted law and calibration independence conditions of Appendix A.5.

For a precise minimax statement, consider the experiment observing only Dn=((Pi,Vi))i=1nD_{n}=((P_{i},V_{i}))_{i=1}^{n}, i.i.d., with Vi=g⁡(Zi)∈[0,1]V_{i}=g(Z_{i})\in[0,1]; an estimator returns a bounded nondecreasing map aDn​(P)a_{D_{n}}(P). No target outcomes, additional target draws or population oracle are available. Any auxiliary input is independent of DnD_{n} and has the same law for every population in the comparison. Let 𝔓δ\mathfrak{P}_{\delta} be the class of laws of (P,V,Y)∈[0,1]3(P,V,Y)\in[0,1]^{3} with ‖𝔼⁡[V−Y∣P]‖22≤δ\|\mathbb{E}[V-Y\mid P]\|_{2}^{2}\leq\delta, for 0≤δ≤1/40\leq\delta\leq 1/4. Write Lℚ​(a)=𝔼ℚ​(a⁡(P)−Y)2L_{\mathbb{Q}}(a)=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{Q}}(a(P)-Y)^{2} and Lℚ∗=infa∈ℳLℚ​(a)=N+I+GL_{\mathbb{Q}}^{*}=\inf_{a\in\mathcal{M}}L_{\mathbb{Q}}(a)=N+I+G. Then

infaDn∈ℳsupℚ∈𝔓δ𝔼[Lℚ(aDn)−Lℚ∗]≍δ+n−2/3.\inf_{a_{D_{n}}\in\mathcal{M}}\sup_{\mathbb{Q}\in\mathfrak{P}_{\delta}}\mathbb{E}\!\left[L_{\mathbb{Q}}(a_{D_{n}})-L_{\mathbb{Q}}^{*}\right]\asymp\delta+n^{-2/3}.

The infimum is over measurable estimators; expectation includes calibration and estimator randomness. The upper bound follows above. Both lower constructions use the same fixed representation Z=(P,V)Z=(P,V) and known probe g⁡(P,V)=Vg(P,V)=V, with auxiliary information identical across alternatives. For bias, take P=V=1/2P=V=1/2 and Y∼Bernoulli⁡(1/2±δ)Y\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(1/2\pm\sqrt{\delta}). The observed law is identical under both signs, and the average excess risk is 𝔼⁡[(aDn​(1/2)−1/2)2]+δ≥δ\mathbb{E}[(a_{D_{n}}(1/2)-1/2)^{2}]+\delta\geq\delta (Le Cam’s two-point method; Yu, 1997).

For fitting, put k=⌈n1/3⌉k=\lceil n^{1/3}\rceil and let PP be uniform on pj=j/(k+1)p_{j}=j/(k+1), j=1,…,kj=1,\ldots,k. Set Y=VY=V and V|P=pj∼Bernoulli⁡(θj)V\mid P=p_{j}\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(\theta_{j}), with θj=1/4+(j−1/2)/(2​k)+εj/(8​k)\theta_{j}=1/4+(j-1/2)/(2k)+\varepsilon_{j}/(8k), εj∈{−1,1}\varepsilon_{j}\in\{-1,1\}. These curves are monotone, lie in [1/4,3/4][1/4,3/4], and have zero probe bias. Scalar excess risk is k−1​∑j(aDn​(pj)−θj)2k^{-1}\sum_{j}(a_{D_{n}}(p_{j})-\theta_{j})^{2}. Neighboring sign models differ by 1/(4​k)1/(4k) at one score and have KL⁡(Dn+,Dn−)≤n/(3​k3)≤1/3\mathrm{KL}(D_{n}^{+},D_{n}^{-})\leq n/(3k^{3})\leq 1/3. Their testing error is bounded away from zero, so summing the coordinate errors gives a lower bound of order k−2≍n−2/3k^{-2}\asymp n^{-2/3} (Yu, 1997), the isotonic minimax order (Zhang, 2002; Guntuboyina and Sen, 2018). The maximum of the two lower bounds controls their sum up to a constant. This is a worst-case result for the specified scalar-calibration experiment, not for serving the richer probe directly, and it supplies neither a bias certificate nor usable constants for a particular fitted probe.

Corollary A.11 (PAIC’s limit and the role of the anchor).

Under Theorem A.10, PAIC’s risk converges to N+I+GN+I+G. It converges to oracle PRCE zero when I=G=0I=G=0. If qq is nondecreasing, the remaining excess risk is II; otherwise pooling contributes GG. Isotonic regression on labels has the same population minimizing class in ℳ¯\overline{\mathcal{M}} as isotonic regression on m⋆m^{\star}.

Proof.

For any two bounded maps, the difference of their squared losses is bounded in expectation by twice their L1L^{1} distance. Hence convergence in (25) gives convergence of risk to L⁡(τiso)=N+I+GL(\tau_{\mathrm{iso}})=N+I+G. The final claim follows from 𝔼​(Y−a⁡(P))2=N+𝔼​(m⋆−a⁡(P))2\mathbb{E}(Y-a(P))^{2}=N+\mathbb{E}(m^{\star}-a(P))^{2}: the term NN does not depend on aa. Probe anchoring can change finite-sample bias and variance, but the population projection argument does not guarantee dominance over label-anchored isotonic regression (Zadrozny and Elkan, 2002). ∎

The weaker assumption can hold without full probe consistency: take Z=YZ=Y a fair bit, P=1/2P=1/2, and gn=1/2g_{n}=1/2. Then bn=0b_{n}=0 and δn=0\delta_{n}=0, but ‖gn−m⋆‖22=1/4\|g_{n}-m^{\star}\|_{2}^{2}=1/4 for every nn. The probe is adequate for the scalar target while ignoring within-score information. Training independence remains essential: a probe that equals one only at continuously distributed calibration observations can have zero population error against m⋆=0m^{\star}=0 while producing all-one fit targets.

Extension to repeated answers.

For i.i.d. calibration clusters, independent of probe training, replace ℚn\mathbb{Q}_{n} by the prompt-level empirical law ℚJ​f=J−1​∑jKj−1​∑if⁡(Zj​i,Yj​i)\mathbb{Q}_{J}f=J^{-1}\sum_{j}K_{j}^{-1}\sum_{i}f(Z_{ji},Y_{ji}) and use the target and norms under (9). For independent uniform answer indices IjI_{j} within the observed clusters, conditional Jensen gives

supH|∑jεj1Kj∑iw(Zj​i)𝟏{Pj​i∈H}|≤𝔼I|CsupH|∑jεjw(Zj​Ij)𝟏{Pj​Ij∈H}|.\sup_{H}\left|\sum_{j}\varepsilon_{j}\frac{1}{K_{j}}\sum_{i}w(Z_{ji})\mathbf{1}\{P_{ji}\in H\}\right|\leq\mathbb{E}_{I\mid C}\sup_{H}\left|\sum_{j}\varepsilon_{j}w(Z_{jI_{j}})\mathbf{1}\{P_{jI_{j}}\in H\}\right|.

After averaging over clusters and indices, the selected answers are i.i.d. under ℚ\mathbb{Q}. The same symmetrization bound applies with JJ in place of nn; the g2g^{2} term is also a bounded independent cluster average. Hence Lemma A.9 and Theorem A.10 hold with the same C0C_{0} and JJ as sample size. Finite random cluster sizes need no moment bound. All training/calibration independence conditions remain. Pooling out-of-fold predictions from different fitted representations requires a separate aggregation argument and compatible feature geometry.

A.6 Residual-corrected risk comparisons and recommendations

The following construction applies prediction-powered mean estimation (Angelopoulos et al., 2023) to paired losses. Unlike an uncorrected PRCE comparison, it uses labels to estimate the probe-error direction relevant to the decision. It does not require probe consistency.

Condition on a fitted probe gg and M≥2M\geq 2 bounded candidate scores, including s0s_{0}. Take two mutually independent samples from the same prompt-cluster law in (T4): JL≥2J_{L}\geq 2 labeled prompts and JU≥2J_{U}\geq 2 prompts whose labels are unobserved. Both samples are independent of all fitting, feature selection, and candidate construction. For a generic cluster C=((Zi,Yi))i=1KC=((Z_{i},Y_{i}))_{i=1}^{K}, define

Aa​b​(C)\displaystyle A_{ab}(C) =1K​∑i[(sa​(Zi)−g⁡(Zi))2−(sb​(Zi)−g⁡(Zi))2],\displaystyle=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{i}\big[(s_{a}(Z_{i})-g(Z_{i}))^{2}-(s_{b}(Z_{i})-g(Z_{i}))^{2}\big], (26)
Da​b​(C)\displaystyle D_{ab}(C) =1K​∑i[(Yi−sa​(Zi))2−(Yi−sb​(Zi))2].\displaystyle=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{i}\big[(Y_{i}-s_{a}(Z_{i}))^{2}-(Y_{i}-s_{b}(Z_{i}))^{2}\big]. (27)

Then 𝔼​Aa​b=Dg​(a,b)\mathbb{E}A_{ab}=D_{g}(a,b) and 𝔼​Da​b=Δa​b\mathbb{E}D_{ab}=\Delta_{ab} under the common induced law ℚ\mathbb{Q}. The exact residual correction is

Da​b​(C)−Aa​b​(C)=2K​∑i(sa​(Zi)−sb​(Zi))​(g⁡(Zi)−Yi).D_{ab}(C)-A_{ab}(C)=\frac{2}{K}\sum_{i}(s_{a}(Z_{i})-s_{b}(Z_{i}))(g(Z_{i})-Y_{i}). (28)

For a fixed λ∈[0,1]\lambda\in[0,1], write

Δ^a​bλ=(Da​b−λ​Aa​b)¯L+λ​A¯U,a​b.\widehat{\Delta}_{ab}^{\lambda}=\overline{(D_{ab}-\lambda A_{ab})}_{L}+\lambda\overline{A}_{U,ab}. (29)

Here and below bars average prompts. The choice λ=1\lambda=1 is the residual-corrected comparison; λ=0\lambda=0 is ordinary paired labeled validation. For each fixed λ\lambda, cancellation of the two proxy expectations proves 𝔼​Δ^a​bλ=Δa​b\mathbb{E}\widehat{\Delta}_{ab}^{\lambda}=\Delta_{ab}. In contrast, PRCE⁡(g,g)=0\mathrm{PRCE}(g;g)=0 automatically makes gg an uncorrected PRCE minimizer if it is an eligible candidate. Independent probe fitting does not remove this self-reference.

An observable mean bound.

For n≥2n\geq 2, unbiased sample variance vv with divisor n−1n-1, known range diameter RR, and 0<ϵ<10<\epsilon<1, let

B⁡(n,v,R,ϵ)=2​v​log⁡(4/ϵ)n+7​R​log⁡(4/ϵ)3​(n−1).B(n,v,R,\epsilon)=\sqrt{\frac{2v\log(4/\epsilon)}{n}}+\frac{7R\log(4/\epsilon)}{3(n-1)}. (30)

For i.i.d. observations in an interval of diameter RR, their mean is within this radius of its expectation with probability at least 1−ϵ1-\epsilon. This follows by rescaling Theorem 4 of Maurer and Pontil (2009) and applying its one-sided bound to both tails at error level ϵ/2\epsilon/2. Their pairwise sample variance equals the usual variance with divisor n−1n-1.

Theorem A.12 (Simultaneous corrected comparisons).

Under the fixed-fitting and two-pool assumptions above, let Λ⊂[0,1]\Lambda\subset[0,1] be a nonempty finite set fixed before comparison. Set H=M⁡(M−1)/2H=M(M-1)/2 and ϵ=α/(2​H​|Λ|)\epsilon=\alpha/(2H|\Lambda|) for 0<α<10<\alpha<1. Let vL,a​bλv_{L,ab}^{\lambda} be the sample variance of Da​b−λ​Aa​bD_{ab}-\lambda A_{ab} across labeled prompts, and vU,a​bv_{U,ab} the sample variance of Aa​bA_{ab} across unlabeled prompts. Define

ra​bλ=B⁡(JL,vL,a​bλ,2​(1+λ),ϵ)+λ​B​(JU,vU,a​b,2,ϵ).r_{ab}^{\lambda}=B(J_{L},v_{L,ab}^{\lambda},2(1+\lambda),\epsilon)+\lambda B(J_{U},v_{U,ab},2,\epsilon). (31)

Conditionally on fitting, with probability at least 1−α1-\alpha,

|Δ^a​bλ−Δa​b|≤ra​bλfor every candidate pair and every ​λ∈Λ.|\widehat{\Delta}_{ab}^{\lambda}-\Delta_{ab}|\leq r_{ab}^{\lambda}\quad\text{for every candidate pair and every }\lambda\in\Lambda. (32)

The event covers selection within the frozen family and grid. It does not make a post-selected point estimate unbiased.

Proof.

Squared losses lie in [0,1][0,1], so Aa​b,Da​b∈[−1,1]A_{ab},D_{ab}\in[-1,1] and Da​b−λ​Aa​b∈[−(1+λ),1+λ]D_{ab}-\lambda A_{ab}\in[-(1+\lambda),1+\lambda]. Apply (30) to the labeled and unlabeled prompt averages for every unordered pair and every grid value. There are at most 2​H​|Λ|2H|\Lambda| events, each failing with probability at most ϵ\epsilon. Their simultaneous success has probability at least 1−α1-\alpha by a union bound; events for different pairs need not be independent. The triangle inequality, expectation cancellation in (29), and reversal of pair signs prove (32). Arbitrary within-prompt dependence and finite random KK are allowed because contributions are bounded cluster averages. ∎

For the main construction use Λ={1}\Lambda=\{1\}, giving ϵ=α/(2​H)\epsilon=\alpha/(2H) and labeled/unlabeled range diameters 44 and 22. For a prespecified labeled-only procedure no unlabeled sample is needed: use D¯L\overline{D}_{L} with radius B⁡(JL,vD,2,α/H)B(J_{L},v_{D},2,\alpha/H). Comparing several separately reported methods does not authorize selecting one afterward while retaining its unadjusted coverage level.

Corollary A.13 (A recommendation with controlled false improvement).

Fix ηmin≥0\eta_{\min}\geq 0. For a fixed permitted weight, select the candidate a≠0a\neq 0 with smallest Ua​0=Δ^a​0λ+ra​0λU_{a0}=\widehat{\Delta}_{a0}^{\lambda}+r_{a0}^{\lambda}, using a predeclared tie order. Recommend it only when Ua​0<−ηminU_{a0}<-\eta_{\min}; otherwise retain s0s_{0} and report an inconclusive comparison. Under Theorem A.12,

Pr⁡{recommend ​a≠0​ with ​L​(sa)≥L⁡(s0)−ηmin∣fitting}≤α.\Pr\{\text{recommend }a\neq 0\text{ with }L(s_{a})\geq L(s_{0})-\eta_{\min}\mid\text{fitting}\}\leq\alpha.

Selection of both the candidate and a weight in the jointly covered Λ\Lambda obeys the same guarantee.

Proof.

On the simultaneous event, Δa​0≤Ua​0<−ηmin\Delta_{a0}\leq U_{a0}<-\eta_{\min} for every accepted recommendation. A false declaration therefore implies failure of that event. This is an unconditional false-declaration probability over comparison samples, not a conditional error rate among recommendations. ∎

When the correction can help.

For a fixed weight, independence of the two pools gives exactly

Var⁡(Δ^a​bλ)=Var⁡(Da​b−λ​Aa​b)JL+λ2​Var⁡(Aa​b)JU.\Var(\widehat{\Delta}_{ab}^{\lambda})=\frac{\Var(D_{ab}-\lambda A_{ab})}{J_{L}}+\frac{\lambda^{2}\Var(A_{ab})}{J_{U}}. (33)

Thus additional unlabeled prompts reduce the proxy contribution, while probe usefulness depends on the residual contribution. If Var⁡(Aa​b)>0\Var(A_{ab})>0, the population variance-minimizing weight in [0,1][0,1] is

λa​b⋆=clip[0,1]⁡Cov⁡(Da​b,Aa​b)(1+JL/JU)​Var⁡(Aa​b).\lambda_{ab}^{\star}=\operatorname{clip}_{[0,1]}\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(D_{ab},A_{ab})}{(1+J_{L}/J_{U})\Var(A_{ab})}.

When Var⁡(Aa​b)=0\Var(A_{ab})=0, all weights have the same variance; choose zero. This is the familiar control-variate calculation underlying power tuning (Angelopoulos et al., 2024). A plug-in weight estimated on the comparison data is not automatically covered by a fixed-weight theorem; use an independently fixed weight or the simultaneous finite-grid result. A common weight gives coherent differences of candidate-risk estimates; pair-specific weights instead define pairwise comparisons.

The finite-sample radius is observable, not necessarily narrow. Its variance term can adapt to small paired differences, but its range term can dominate at small JLJ_{L}. A valid known bound ‖sa−sb‖∞≤d≤1\|s_{a}-s_{b}\|_{\infty}\leq d\leq 1 permits replacing the absolute bound 11 for Aa​b,Da​bA_{ab},D_{ab} by 2​d−d22d-d^{2}: factor the difference of squares and maximize over two scores at distance at most dd and a target in [0,1][0,1]. This can tighten the range diameters, but an observed maximum does not bound unobserved values. If labeled and unlabeled pools are the same observations with the same weights, (29) reduces algebraically to D¯L\overline{D}_{L} for every λ\lambda; the independent-pool variance formula no longer applies. Neither correction nor a small probe error guarantees a label-efficiency or runtime advantage.

A.7 Directional adoption by betting

The intervals above cover every pairwise contrast in both directions. Adopting a candidate requires less: evidence that it lowers risk relative to the unchanged score. The following test uses a standard betting construction (Waudby-Smith and Ramdas, 2024). It controls false adoption.

Condition on the fitted probe and the frozen candidate family, and let HH count the non-original candidates. For candidate hh and an independent labeled prompt jj with KjK_{j} answers, write

Dj​h\displaystyle D_{jh} =1Kj​∑i=1Kj[(Yj​i−h⁡(Zj​i))2−(Yj​i−Pj​i)2],\displaystyle=\frac{1}{K_{j}}\sum_{i=1}^{K_{j}}\big[(Y_{ji}-h(Z_{ji}))^{2}-(Y_{ji}-P_{ji})^{2}\big],
Aj​h\displaystyle A_{jh} =1Kj​∑i=1Kj[(h⁡(Zj​i)−g⁡(Zj​i))2−(Pj​i−g⁡(Zj​i))2],\displaystyle=\frac{1}{K_{j}}\sum_{i=1}^{K_{j}}\big[(h(Z_{ji})-g(Z_{ji}))^{2}-(P_{ji}-g(Z_{ji}))^{2}\big],

so that 𝔼​Dj​h=L⁡(h)−L⁡(P)\mathbb{E}D_{jh}=L(h)-L(P) under ℚ\mathbb{Q}. Let δh∈[0,1]\delta_{h}\in[0,1] satisfy δh≥supz|h⁡(z)−s0​(z)|\delta_{h}\geq\sup_{z}|h(z)-s_{0}(z)|; this must be a certified bound over the whole input domain, not an observed maximum. Two scores within δh\delta_{h} of each other and a target in [0,1][0,1] have squared losses differing by at most Bh=δh​(2−δh)B_{h}=\delta_{h}(2-\delta_{h}): factor the difference of squares and maximize, as in Appendix A.6. Hence |Dj​h|,|Aj​h|≤Bh|D_{jh}|,|A_{jh}|\leq B_{h}.

Proposition A.14 (Adoption by betting).

Condition on fitting, and let the nn labeled prompts be i.i.d. and independent of fitting. Fix 0<α<10<\alpha<1 and a nonempty finite set 𝒮⊂[0,1)\mathcal{S}\subset[0,1). For each non-original candidate with Bh>0B_{h}>0, let

Eh​(s)=∏j=1n(1−s​Dj​hBh),Eh=1|𝒮|​∑s∈𝒮Eh​(s).E_{h}(s)=\prod_{j=1}^{n}\Big(1-s\,\frac{D_{jh}}{B_{h}}\Big),\qquad E_{h}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{S}|}\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}}E_{h}(s).

Then

Pr⁡{∃h:L⁡(h)≥L⁡(P)​and​Eh≥H/α}≤α.\Pr\big\{\exists h:\ L(h)\geq L(P)\ \text{and}\ E_{h}\geq H/\alpha\big\}\leq\alpha.

Consequently, the rule that certifies every candidate with Eh≥H/αE_{h}\geq H/\alpha, adopts the certified candidate with the smallest mean D¯h\overline{D}_{h} under a fixed tie order, and otherwise retains PP, adopts a candidate with L⁡(h)≥L⁡(P)L(h)\geq L(P) with probability at most α\alpha.

Proof.

Fix hh with L⁡(h)≥L⁡(P)L(h)\geq L(P), so 𝔼​Dj​h≥0\mathbb{E}D_{jh}\geq 0. For s∈𝒮s\in\mathcal{S}, each factor satisfies 1−s​Dj​h/Bh≥1−s>01-sD_{jh}/B_{h}\geq 1-s>0 because |Dj​h|≤Bh|D_{jh}|\leq B_{h}, and its expectation is 1−s​𝔼​Dj​h/Bh≤11-s\mathbb{E}D_{jh}/B_{h}\leq 1. Prompts are independent, so 𝔼​Eh​(s)=∏j𝔼⁡(1−s​Dj​h/Bh)≤1\mathbb{E}E_{h}(s)=\prod_{j}\mathbb{E}(1-sD_{jh}/B_{h})\leq 1, and averaging over 𝒮\mathcal{S} gives 𝔼​Eh≤1\mathbb{E}E_{h}\leq 1. Markov’s inequality gives Pr{Eh≥H/α}≤α/H\Pr\{E_{h}\geq H/\alpha\}\leq\alpha/H, and a union bound over at most HH such candidates proves the claim. A candidate with Bh=0B_{h}=0 coincides with PP and is never certified. ∎

The main text and experiments use 𝒮={0.05,0.1,0.25,0.5,0.9}\mathcal{S}=\{0.05,0.1,0.25,0.5,0.9\}. The guarantee applies to one prespecified method and comparison; choosing a method or budget after inspecting a sweep is not covered.

A proxy-assisted variant.

Condition on fitting and prespecify disjoint groups. Each group contains one labeled prompt and a fixed positive number rr of unlabeled prompts. All these prompt clusters are mutually independent, sampled from the same target cluster law, and independent of fitting; their prompt-weighted answer law is ℚ\mathbb{Q}. For fixed λ∈[0,1]\lambda\in[0,1], form

D~j​h,λ=Dj​h−λ​Aj​h+λ​A¯j​h𝒰,\widetilde{D}_{jh,\lambda}=D_{jh}-\lambda A_{jh}+\lambda\overline{A}^{\mathcal{U}}_{jh},
