The zero-weight component gives a valid fallback but pays a mixture penalty.

A.8 Kernel identities and their scope

The kernel step maps a conditional-mean residual into a collection of testable moments. For attribution, take the product kernel k~​((z,y),(z′,y′))=k⁡(z,z′)​y​y′\widetilde{k}((z,y),(z^{\prime},y^{\prime}))=k(z,z^{\prime})yy^{\prime} in the distribution-matching framework of Marx et al. (2023). Compare the law of (Z,Y)(Z,Y) with a law of (Z,Y~)(Z,\widetilde{Y}) having the same ZZ marginal and 𝔼⁡[Y~∣Z]=s⁡(Z)\mathbb{E}[\widetilde{Y}\mid Z]=s(Z), with Y~∈[0,1]\widetilde{Y}\in[0,1]. Their difference of mean embeddings is 𝔼⁡[(Y−s⁡(Z))​Φ​(Z)]\mathbb{E}[(Y-s(Z))\Phi(Z)]. Its squared norm is the SKCE below; for graded outcomes this specializes distribution matching to conditional means.

Define the corresponding residual functional by

SCFk​(s):=supf∈ℋk‖f‖ℋk≤1|𝔼⁡[(Y−s⁡(Z))​f​(Z)]|.\mathrm{SCF}_{k}(s):=\sup_{\begin{subarray}{c}f\in\mathcal{H}_{k}\\ \|f\|_{\mathcal{H}_{k}}\leq 1\end{subarray}}|\mathbb{E}[(Y-s(Z))f(Z)]|. (34)
Theorem A.15 (Residual norm identity and zero identification).

Under (T1) and the bounded-RKHS part of (T3), put r=Y−s⁡(Z)r=Y-s(Z) and μs=𝔼⁡[r​Φ​(Z)]\mu_{s}=\mathbb{E}[r\Phi(Z)]. For independent primed copies,

SKCEk​(s)=𝔼⁡[r​r′​k​(Z,Z′)]=‖μs‖ℋk2=SCFk​(s)2.\mathrm{SKCE}_{k}(s)=\mathbb{E}[rr^{\prime}k(Z,Z^{\prime})]=\|\mu_{s}\|_{\mathcal{H}_{k}}^{2}=\mathrm{SCF}_{k}(s)^{2}.

If ℋk\mathcal{H}_{k} is dense in L2​(ℚZ)L^{2}(\mathbb{Q}_{Z}), then SKCEk​(s)=0\mathrm{SKCE}_{k}(s)=0 if and only if s=m⋆s=m^{\star} almost surely.

Proof.

The bound ‖r​Φ​(Z)‖≤κ\|r\Phi(Z)\|\leq\sqrt{\kappa} makes the Bochner mean well defined. The reproducing property and independence give

𝔼⁡[r​r′​k​(Z,Z′)]=𝔼⁡⟨r​Φ​(Z),r′​Φ​(Z′)⟩=⟨μs,μs⟩.\mathbb{E}[rr^{\prime}k(Z,Z^{\prime})]=\mathbb{E}\langle r\Phi(Z),r^{\prime}\Phi(Z^{\prime})\rangle=\langle\mu_{s},\mu_{s}\rangle.

For f∈ℋkf\in\mathcal{H}_{k}, 𝔼⁡[r​f​(Z)]=⟨μs,f⟩\mathbb{E}[rf(Z)]=\langle\mu_{s},f\rangle. Cauchy–Schwarz gives a supremum of ‖μs‖\|\mu_{s}\| over the unit ball; when μs≠0\mu_{s}\neq 0 it is attained at μs/‖μs‖\mu_{s}/\|\mu_{s}\|, and when μs=0\mu_{s}=0 every value is zero. These are the usual mean-embedding identities (Gretton et al., 2012; Muandet et al., 2017). Related kernel calibration criteria use distribution matching (Marx et al., 2023); the identity here specifically concerns the residual-weighted mean embedding.

Conditioning on ZZ writes the moment as 𝔼⁡[(m⋆−s)​f​(Z)]\mathbb{E}[(m^{\star}-s)f(Z)]. If it vanishes for every RKHS function, density and m⋆−s∈L2​(ℚZ)m^{\star}-s\in L^{2}(\mathbb{Q}_{Z}) imply ‖m⋆−s‖22=0\|m^{\star}-s\|_{2}^{2}=0. The converse is immediate. On a compact metric space, continuous universality supplies this density through density of continuous functions in L2L^{2} (Sriperumbudur et al., 2011). The relevant residual measure is signed, so injectivity stated only for probability measures is not, by itself, the required argument. ∎

Theorem A.16 (Upper bound by oracle PRCE and continuity).

Under the bounded-RKHS conditions above, for bounded ZZ-measurable scores s,ts,t,

0≤SKCEk​(s)\displaystyle 0\leq\mathrm{SKCE}_{k}(s) ≤κ​PRCE​(s,m⋆),\displaystyle\leq\kappa\mathrm{PRCE}(s;m^{\star}), (35)
|SKCEk​(s)−SKCEk​(t)|\displaystyle|\sqrt{\mathrm{SKCE}_{k}(s)}-\sqrt{\mathrm{SKCE}_{k}(t)}| ≤κ​‖s−t‖2.\displaystyle\leq\sqrt{\kappa}\,\|s-t\|_{2}. (36)

Universality is unnecessary for either statement.

Proof.

𝔼⁡[(Y−m⋆)​Φ​(Z)]=0\mathbb{E}[(Y-m^{\star})\Phi(Z)]=0, so μs=𝔼⁡[(m⋆−s)​Φ​(Z)]\mu_{s}=\mathbb{E}[(m^{\star}-s)\Phi(Z)]. Consequently,

‖μs‖≤κ​𝔼​|m⋆−s|≤κ​‖m⋆−s‖2.\|\mu_{s}\|\leq\sqrt{\kappa}\,\mathbb{E}|m^{\star}-s|\leq\sqrt{\kappa}\,\|m^{\star}-s\|_{2}.

Square to obtain the first bound. For the second, use the reverse triangle inequality followed by ‖μs−μt‖=‖𝔼⁡[(t−s)​Φ​(Z)]‖≤κ​‖s−t‖2\|\mu_{s}-\mu_{t}\|=\|\mathbb{E}[(t-s)\Phi(Z)]\|\leq\sqrt{\kappa}\|s-t\|_{2}. ∎

Proposition A.17 (Kernel control of comparison bias).

Under (T1) and the bounded-RKHS conditions in (T3), fix sa,sb,gs_{a},s_{b},g under one population law. If w=sa−sb∈ℋkw=s_{a}-s_{b}\in\mathcal{H}_{k}, then

|Dg​(a,b)−Δa​b|≤2​‖w‖ℋk​SKCEk​(g).|D_{g}(a,b)-\Delta_{ab}|\leq 2\|w\|_{\mathcal{H}_{k}}\sqrt{\mathrm{SKCE}_{k}(g)}. (37)

For any v∈ℋkv\in\mathcal{H}_{k} approximating ww in L2L^{2},

|Dg​(a,b)−Δa​b|≤2​‖v‖ℋk​SKCEk​(g)+2​‖w−v‖2​‖g−m⋆‖2.|D_{g}(a,b)-\Delta_{ab}|\leq 2\|v\|_{\mathcal{H}_{k}}\sqrt{\mathrm{SKCE}_{k}(g)}+2\|w-v\|_{2}\|g-m^{\star}\|_{2}.
Proof.

For μg=𝔼⁡[(Y−g)​Φ​(Z)]\mu_{g}=\mathbb{E}[(Y-g)\Phi(Z)], the paired identity gives Dg−Δa​b=2​𝔼​[(Y−g)​w​(Z)]=2​⟨μg,w⟩D_{g}-\Delta_{ab}=2\mathbb{E}[(Y-g)w(Z)]=2\langle\mu_{g},w\rangle. Apply RKHS Cauchy–Schwarz and Theorem A.15. For the second statement, split w=v+(w−v)w=v+(w-v) and condition the remainder on ZZ, then use L2L^{2} Cauchy–Schwarz. This is a decision-specific specialization of residual/kernel loss control (Marx et al., 2023); it audits the probe, not the chosen candidate’s residuals. ∎

A finite Nyström space need not contain nonlinear or isotonic candidate contrasts. One alternative, fixed after candidate fitting but before comparison, is a finite kernel spanning those contrasts: k𝒮​(z,z′)=H−1​∑a<bwa​b​(z)​wa​b​(z′)k_{\mathcal{S}}(z,z^{\prime})=H^{-1}\sum_{a<b}w_{ab}(z)w_{ab}(z^{\prime}). It has diagonal at most one and RKHS contrast norms at most H\sqrt{H}. Its SKCE tests precisely the selected residual moments, not every feature-conditioned error. A quantitative use of (37) needs an upper bound on SKCE, not merely failure to reject its zero null.

Theorem A.18 (Limiting SKCE after PAIC).

Under Theorem A.10 and (T3),

SKCEk​(τ^n∘s0)⟶SKCEk​(τiso∘s0)≤κ⁡(I+G)\mathrm{SKCE}_{k}(\hat{\tau}_{n}\circ s_{0})\longrightarrow\mathrm{SKCE}_{k}(\tau_{\mathrm{iso}}\circ s_{0})\leq\kappa(I+G)

in probability and in mean. This is a limiting upper bound, not a guarantee that recalibration decreases SKCE.

Proof.

Apply (36) to the two composed scores. Each square root is at most κ\sqrt{\kappa}, so the difference of the SKCE values is at most 2​κ​‖τ^n−τiso‖22\kappa\|\hat{\tau}_{n}-\tau_{\mathrm{iso}}\|_{2}. Theorem A.10 gives the asserted convergence. The limiting bound uses Theorem A.16 and PRCE⁡(τiso∘s0,m⋆)=I+G\mathrm{PRCE}(\tau_{\mathrm{iso}}\circ s_{0};m^{\star})=I+G. ∎

Remark A.19 (Kernel dependence, approximation, and tolerance claims).

Exact zero identification does not make nonzero tolerances kernel-free. For equiprobable Z∈{0,1}Z\in\{0,1\}, let Y=ZY=Z and s=1/2s=1/2. The normalized kernel matrix

Kρ=(1ρρ1),0≤ρ<1,K_{\rho}=\begin{pmatrix}1&\rho\\ \rho&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad 0\leq\rho<1,

is universal on this finite space, yet SKCEKρ​(s)=(1−ρ)/8\mathrm{SKCE}_{K_{\rho}}(s)=(1-\rho)/8 while PRCE⁡(s,m⋆)=1/4\mathrm{PRCE}(s;m^{\star})=1/4. The kernel can make the former arbitrarily small without changing the latter. Thus neither normalization nor universality supplies a kernel-uniform inverse bound. For a fixed finite feature map, including a Nyström approximation, the norm identity continues to hold but zero tests only those feature moments. Full identification does not follow automatically.

PAIC need not minimize SKCE either. Let Y=Z∈{0,1}Y=Z\in\{0,1\} with state probabilities (1/4,3/4)(1/4,3/4), s0=9/10s_{0}=9/10, and k(z,z′)=𝟏{z=z′}k(z,z^{\prime})=\mathbf{1}\{z=z^{\prime}\}. With oracle anchor g=m⋆g=m^{\star}, population PAIC gives 3/43/4, lowering risk from 21/10021/100 to 3/163/16, while increasing SKCE from 9/1609/160 to 9/1289/128. The residual IPM and its square have the same minimizers. Squaring provides the quadratic form used by the unbiased pair estimator; the norm identity computes the witness supremum directly.

A.9 Inference with independent prompt clusters

Let ζj=Kj−1​∑i(Yj​i−s⁡(Zj​i))​Φ​(Zj​i)\zeta_{j}=K_{j}^{-1}\sum_{i}(Y_{ji}-s(Z_{ji}))\Phi(Z_{ji}), μ=𝔼​ζj\mu=\mathbb{E}\zeta_{j}, and C=𝔼⁡[(ζj−μ)⊗(ζj−μ)]C=\mathbb{E}[(\zeta_{j}-\mu)\otimes(\zeta_{j}-\mu)]. Here u⊗vu\otimes v is the operator w↦⟨v,w⟩​uw\mapsto\langle v,w\rangle u. Because ‖ζj‖≤κ\|\zeta_{j}\|\leq\sqrt{\kappa}, CC is trace-class. In this subsection θ=‖μ‖2\theta=\|\mu\|^{2} is SKCE under the law in (9).

Theorem A.20 (Prompt-cluster U-statistic).

Under (T3) and (T4),

UJ=1J⁡(J−1)​∑j≠ℓ⟨ζj,ζℓ⟩U_{J}=\frac{1}{J(J-1)}\sum_{j\neq\ell}\langle\zeta_{j},\zeta_{\ell}\rangle

is unbiased for θ\theta. If σ2=4​Var⁡⟨ζ1,μ⟩>0\sigma^{2}=4\Var\langle\zeta_{1},\mu\rangle>0, then J​(UJ−θ)⇒𝒩⁡(0,σ2)\sqrt{J}(U_{J}-\theta)\Rightarrow\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}). Under μ=0\mu=0, with (λb)(\lambda_{b}) the eigenvalues of CC,

J​UJ⇒WC:=∑b≥1λb​(Gb2−1),Gb∼iid𝒩⁡(0,1).JU_{J}\ \Rightarrow\ W_{C}:=\sum_{b\geq 1}\lambda_{b}(G_{b}^{2}-1),\qquad G_{b}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{iid}}}{{\sim}}\mathcal{N}(0,1). (38)

The eigenvalues are those of the residual-weighted cluster covariance, not of the bare semantic kernel.

Proof.

Different prompt clusters are independent, hence every off-diagonal summand has expectation ⟨μ,μ⟩\langle\mu,\mu\rangle. Write vj=ζj−μv_{j}=\zeta_{j}-\mu. The Hoeffding decomposition (Hoeffding, 1948) is

UJ−θ=2J​∑j⟨vj,μ⟩+1J⁡(J−1)​∑j≠ℓ⟨vj,vℓ⟩.U_{J}-\theta=\frac{2}{J}\sum_{j}\langle v_{j},\mu\rangle+\frac{1}{J(J-1)}\sum_{j\neq\ell}\langle v_{j},v_{\ell}\rangle.

The second term has variance 2​𝔼​⟨v1,v2⟩2/[J⁡(J−1)]2\mathbb{E}\langle v_{1},v_{2}\rangle^{2}/[J(J-1)]; multiplied by J\sqrt{J}, it vanishes in mean square. The ordinary scalar CLT applies to the first term when its variance is positive.

Under the null, μ=0\mu=0 and the exact identity is

JUJ=JJ−1[‖J−1/2∑jζj‖2−1J∑j∥ζj∥2].JU_{J}=\frac{J}{J-1}\left[\left\|J^{-1/2}\sum_{j}\zeta_{j}\right\|^{2}-\frac{1}{J}\sum_{j}\|\zeta_{j}\|^{2}\right].

Finite-dimensional projection CLTs and the tail bound 𝔼∥J−1/2∑j(I−Πd)ζj∥2=tr((I−Πd)C)→0\mathbb{E}\|J^{-1/2}\sum_{j}(I-\Pi_{d})\zeta_{j}\|^{2}=\operatorname{tr}((I-\Pi_{d})C)\to 0 give the Hilbert-space Gaussian limit with covariance CC. The strong law gives convergence of the subtracted average to tr⁡C\operatorname{tr}C. Diagonalizing CC yields (38). The series converges since ∑bλb=tr⁡C<∞\sum_{b}\lambda_{b}=\operatorname{tr}C<\infty; in particular the centered series converges in mean square. ∎

Remark A.21 (Degeneracy, diagonals, and sibling answers).

The U-statistic can be negative although θ≥0\theta\geq 0. The empirical squared mean VJ=‖J−1​∑jζj‖2V_{J}=\|J^{-1}\sum_{j}\zeta_{j}\|^{2} instead satisfies

UJ=JJ−1​VJ−∑j‖ζj‖2J⁡(J−1).U_{J}=\frac{J}{J-1}V_{J}-\frac{\sum_{j}\|\zeta_{j}\|^{2}}{J(J-1)}.

Under the null, J​VJJV_{J} has an uncentered weighted chi-squared limit; J​UJJU_{J} has the centered limit in (38). Agreement of two computations of VJV_{J} does not verify this diagonal correction. Also, θ>0\theta>0 alone does not ensure σ2>0\sigma^{2}>0: for equiprobable binary ZZ, Y=1Y=1, s=0s=0, and k(z,z′)=𝟏{z=z′}k(z,z^{\prime})=\mathbf{1}\{z=z^{\prime}\}, θ=1/2\theta=1/2 but ⟨ζ,μ⟩=1/2\langle\zeta,\mu\rangle=1/2 is constant when each cluster contains one answer.

If there are K≥2K\geq 2 answers per prompt, an all-row-pairs statistic also includes sibling pairs. Let γ\gamma be the average expected summand over two distinct answers within one prompt. Counting ordered pairs gives

𝔼⁡[Urows]=θ+K−1J​K−1​(γ−θ).\mathbb{E}[U_{\mathrm{rows}}]=\theta+\frac{K-1}{JK-1}(\gamma-\theta).

This bias is generally nonzero and is of the same order as the null statistic. Excluding within-prompt pairs matches the estimator to the independent sampling unit; grouping cross-validation folds alone does not change which pairs enter the statistic.

The construction below uses one multiplier per independent prompt, in the spirit of wild-bootstrap tests for kernel statistics (Chwialkowski et al., 2014). Its validity is proved for the present centered cluster statistic rather than inferred from a row-level test.

Theorem A.22 (A centered Gaussian multiplier test).

Under the null and conditions of Theorem A.20, let ζ¯=J−1​∑jζj\bar{\zeta}=J^{-1}\sum_{j}\zeta_{j}, xj=ζj−ζ¯x_{j}=\zeta_{j}-\bar{\zeta}, and draw one independent ej∼𝒩⁡(0,1)e_{j}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1) per prompt. Set

TJ∗=1J−1​∑j≠ℓej​eℓ​⟨xj,xℓ⟩.T_{J}^{*}=\frac{1}{J-1}\sum_{j\neq\ell}e_{j}e_{\ell}\langle x_{j},x_{\ell}\rangle.

Its conditional law converges weakly almost surely to the law of WCW_{C}. If C≠0C\neq 0, rejecting when J​UJJU_{J} exceeds its conditional (1−α)(1-\alpha) quantile has pointwise asymptotic size α\alpha, for 0<α<10<\alpha<1. For Monte Carlo quantiles, the number of multiplier draws must also grow to obtain this exact asymptotic statement.

Proof.

Put C^J=J−1​∑jxj⊗xj\widehat{C}_{J}=J^{-1}\sum_{j}x_{j}\otimes x_{j} and BJ∗=J−1/2∑jejxjB_{J}^{*}=J^{-1/2}\sum_{j}e_{j}x_{j}. Conditional on the observations, BJ∗B_{J}^{*} is Gaussian with covariance C^J\widehat{C}_{J}, and

TJ∗=JJ−1​[‖BJ∗‖2−tr⁡C^J−1J​∑j(ej2−1)​‖xj‖2].T_{J}^{*}=\frac{J}{J-1}\left[\|B_{J}^{*}\|^{2}-\operatorname{tr}\widehat{C}_{J}-\frac{1}{J}\sum_{j}(e_{j}^{2}-1)\|x_{j}\|^{2}\right].

Empirical covariance operators converge to CC in trace norm almost surely. To see this here, apply the strong law to finite-rank matrix entries and to squared norms. The trace in the complementary projection can be made arbitrarily small; off-diagonal blocks are controlled by Cauchy–Schwarz. Subtracting the empirical mean contributes a rank-one term converging to the corresponding population term. Thus the conditional law of the first two terms converges weakly almost surely to ‖B‖2−tr⁡C=WC\|B\|^{2}-\operatorname{tr}C=W_{C} for B∼𝒩⁡(0,C)B\sim\mathcal{N}(0,C), by the same finite-projection and trace-tail argument. The last term has conditional variance

2J2​∑j‖xj‖4≤32​κ2J,\frac{2}{J^{2}}\sum_{j}\|x_{j}\|^{4}\leq\frac{32\kappa^{2}}{J},

so it vanishes. If C≠0C\neq 0, at least one nonzero λb​Gb2\lambda_{b}G_{b}^{2} has a density positive on (0,∞)(0,\infty). The sum of the remaining nonnegative terms has positive probability arbitrarily near zero: make finitely many Gaussian coordinates small, then use summability of the eigenvalues and Markov’s inequality for the independent tail. Convolution therefore gives a continuous CDF strictly increasing on (−tr⁡C,∞)(-\operatorname{tr}C,\infty), and hence unique interior quantiles. Quantile convergence and Theorem A.20 give asymptotic size. If C=0C=0 under the null, ζj=0\zeta_{j}=0 almost surely; use strict rejection and never reject the identically zero statistic. ∎

Proposition A.23 (A finite-sample upper bound for a fixed kernel).

Under (T3) and (T4), let VJ=‖J−1​∑jζj‖2V_{J}=\|J^{-1}\sum_{j}\zeta_{j}\|^{2} and θ=‖𝔼​ζj‖2\theta=\|\mathbb{E}\zeta_{j}\|^{2}. For 0<α<10<\alpha<1, with probability at least 1−α1-\alpha,

θ≤[VJ+κJ​(1+2​log⁡(1/α))]2.\theta\leq\left[\sqrt{V_{J}}+\sqrt{\frac{\kappa}{J}}\left(1+\sqrt{2\log(1/\alpha)}\right)\right]^{2}. (39)

This bound concerns the declared kernel only and is not an inverse bound on oracle PRCE.

Proof.

Write F=‖J−1​∑jζj−μ‖F=\|J^{-1}\sum_{j}\zeta_{j}-\mu\|. Independence and centering give 𝔼​F≤𝔼​F2≤κ/J\mathbb{E}F\leq\sqrt{\mathbb{E}F^{2}}\leq\sqrt{\kappa/J}. Replacing one cluster changes FF by at most 2​κ/J2\sqrt{\kappa}/J. The bounded-differences inequality (McDiarmid, 1998) therefore gives F≤κ/J+2​κ​log⁡(1/α)/JF\leq\sqrt{\kappa/J}+\sqrt{2\kappa\log(1/\alpha)/J} with probability at least 1−α1-\alpha. Since ‖μ‖≤VJ+F\|\mu\|\leq\sqrt{V_{J}}+F, squaring proves the claim. ∎

Interpreting an audit.

The point-null test asks whether the selected feature moments reveal residual error. Establishing a tolerance θ<ε\theta<\varepsilon instead requires a one-sided procedure for H0:θ≥εH_{0}:\theta\geq\varepsilon, with a prespecified kernel, threshold, and valid uncertainty control. Non-rejection of the point null does not establish that tolerance or small oracle PRCE. Proposition A.23 supplies one conservative alternative: declare θ<ε\theta<\varepsilon only when its upper bound is below the prespecified ε\varepsilon. Combine its error budget with that of any simultaneous candidate comparisons when using Proposition A.17. Repeated testing over time needs a multiple-testing or sequential policy; the theorem conditions on a fixed score, kernel, and population law.

A.10 Repair classes and relation to prior work

Inputs define what a repair can change.

Suppose ZZ contains every input used by the compared predictors and all risks use the same outcome and population law. A global scalar map τ⁡(P)\tau(P) assigns the same output whenever PP agrees. A group-dependent map τγ⁡(Z)​(P)\tau_{\gamma(Z)}(P) additionally uses a group assignment γ⁡(Z)\gamma(Z). When the group is not determined by PP, it can distinguish answers that no function of PP alone can distinguish. Each group map may be nondecreasing without preserving order across groups. Both outputs are scalars: the distinction is their input restriction, not output dimension. If a candidate uses features outside the declared ZZ, augment the information set before applying the common-target identities.

Chen et al. (2024, Section 4) learn a supervised tree partition from LLM top-layer query embeddings, using a squared-loss criterion on correctness labels, and then fit a separate label-based isotonic regressor within each group. Their groups are learned, not restricted to supplied demographic categories. The deployed correction needs the group assignment. PAIC instead fits one global map of PP to predictions from an independently trained correctness probe. Table 1 separates these choices from direct feature-based prediction.

Melo et al. (2026) develop partition-based estimators of grouping loss and excess decision risk, with local confidence audits and LLM cascades. Their work already connects errors hidden by average calibration to downstream decisions. Our guarantees address a different set of objects: the conditional probe bias affecting a global monotone map, paired risk contrasts between frozen candidates, and residual moments with dependent answers grouped by prompt.

All rows require accounting for fitting and tuning labels. PAIC’s map does not see its fitting prompts’ labels, but its probe is label-trained. The table describes the correction’s inputs, not the cost of obtaining PP, which may already require learned features. A score-only constraint must be declared before comparisons. Enlarging a population predictor class cannot worsen its optimal risk, but finite fitted methods can differ in approximation and estimation error. A richer fitted predictor beating a scalar fit does not identify II (Appendix A.3).

Grouping loss and monotone pooling.

For any measurable repair output Tτ=τ⁡(P)T_{\tau}=\tau(P), conditional variance decomposition gives

𝔼⁡[Var⁡(m⋆∣Tτ)]=I+𝔼⁡[Var⁡(q⁡(P)∣Tτ)].\mathbb{E}[\Var(m^{\star}\mid T_{\tau})]=I+\mathbb{E}[\Var(q(P)\mid T_{\tau})].

This is the squared-loss form of the recalibration identity in Perez-Lebel et al. (2023, Appendix C.10). A noninjective map can add grouping loss; an invertible map preserves it. For the ideal monotone output T=τiso​(P)T=\tau_{\rm iso}(P), Theorem A.4 establishes 𝔼⁡[q⁡(P)∣T]=T\mathbb{E}[q(P)\mid T]=T, so the additional term is exactly GG. The result connects monotone pooling to this established information-loss identity.

Probe targets and the role of the guarantee.

Label-isotonic and PAIC optimize over the same monotone class but fit different targets. Conditional on probe training, qg​(P)=𝔼⁡[g⁡(Z)∣P]q_{g}(P)=\mathbb{E}[g(Z)\mid P] determines the population probe-loss minimizer. Theorem A.10 bounds the label-risk excess over N+I+GN+I+G by (‖bn‖2+un)2(\|b_{n}\|_{2}+\sqrt{u_{n}})^{2} and controls the fitting term under independent calibration sampling. Vanishing score-conditional bias is sufficient for convergence to the monotone benchmark; it neither removes I+GI+G nor guarantees finite-sample superiority over label-isotonic or group-dependent calibration. In particular, greater agreement with the training probe is not evidence of such superiority.

Comparison and audit are separate from candidate construction.

The labeled residual correction applies prediction-powered inference (Angelopoulos et al., 2023; Angelopoulos et al., 2024) to paired squared losses; Theorem A.12 instantiates empirical Bernstein bounds (Maurer and Pontil, 2009) for frozen candidates and independent prompt pools. It can compare scalar and feature-dependent candidates without requiring any one of them to be correct. Its coverage does not promise narrow intervals or lower label cost. The residual embedding is an established kernel construction (Widmann et al., 2019; Marx et al., 2023). Our Theorems A.20 and A.22 specify cross-prompt products and centered multipliers for dependent sibling answers. Groupwise fitting uses labels to change predictions; an independent audit uses labels to test mean-error structure in the selected predictor. These different roles require separate evidence, not a common proxy score treated as ground truth.

Appendix B Experimental details and additional results

This appendix gives the design, results and uncertainty conventions for the experiments of Section 4, in the order of the main text. Appendix C reports the fixed-choice study of Section 4.1.

B.1 Data, scores and uncertainty

Cached answers and loss.

We evaluate confidence scores for eight sampled answers per prompt from Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct on GSM8K (7,3537{,}353 prompts per model), MATH (5,7295{,}729) and a mixed-domain collection of 10,00010{,}000 questions. GSM8K and MATH labels are binary final-answer matches from a fixed parser; 10K labels are automated grades in [0,1][0,1]. Risk averages squared loss within each prompt and then equally across prompts. Each labeled prompt therefore supplies eight answer labels and forms one sampling unit. The loss is Brier loss for binary outcomes and mean squared error for graded outcomes.

Three score regimes.

The raw likelihood score is P=exp⁡(−mean answer-token NLL)P=\exp(-\text{mean answer-token NLL}), where NLL denotes negative log-likelihood. Its probes use a fixed, label-independent 64-coordinate random-sign projection of the final answer state plus eight likelihood summaries, standardized on source fitting data. A learned GSM8K-trained scorer, with 32 learned coordinates, is transferred to MATH in Appendix B.6. The archived learned score is a previously trained and temperature-recalibrated supervised score on GSM8K and 10K. It tests the additional benefit of scalar repair after supervised calibration. These regimes use different fitted functions and should be interpreted separately.

Data separation.

Fitting, unlabeled adaptation, labeled comparison, discovery, audit and test roles are prompt-disjoint; all answers from a prompt stay together. Fitted candidates, maps and thresholds were saved before evaluation outcomes were joined. The cached answer pools had already been used in earlier analyses, so these evaluations are retrospective.

Uncertainty.

The three refits, repeated allocations and seed/fold blocks overlap; their means and ranges are descriptive. Unless stated otherwise, paired prompt-bootstrap intervals are pointwise and conditional on the fitted functions. The archived-score analyses cover four dataset/model cells, three seeds, five folds and three nested fitting budgets, giving 180 settings. Each block contains 147–200 comparison prompts, 73–100 discovery prompts and 75–100 audit prompts.

B.2 Controlled PAIC fitting with equally accurate probes

We test why probes with the same mean squared error can produce different scalar repairs. The key distinction is whether their errors cancel within each score level or leave a persistent bias. Using three constructed probes with known population risks, we separate score-conditional bias from finite-sample fitting error in Theorem 3.2. This controlled study uses no learned probes or LLM predictions.

Population and targets.

The four states (S,H)∈{0.35,0.65}×{−1,1}(S,H)\in\{0.35,0.65\}\times\{-1,1\} are equally likely. The variable SS determines the score level, while HH distinguishes two groups at that level. Their correctness probability is m=S+0.10​Hm=S+0.10H, and Y|S,H∼Bernoulli⁡(m)Y\mid S,H\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(m). The reported score P=S+0.02P=S+0.02 assigns the same confidence to both groups. We evaluate outcome risks analytically, without sampling outcomes. Here N=0.2175N=0.2175, I=0.01I=0.01, and G=0G=0. The optimal scalar and monotone map is P↦SP\mapsto S, with risk N+I=0.2275N+I=0.2275; the unchanged score has risk 0.22790.2279. The three probes are

g−=m−0.08​H,goffset=m+0.08,g+=m+0.08​H.g_{-}=m-0.08H,\qquad g_{\rm offset}=m+0.08,\qquad g_{+}=m+0.08H.

All lie in [0,1][0,1] and have the same excess outcome MSE 𝔼⁡[(g−m)2]=0.0064\mathbb{E}[(g-m)^{2}]=0.0064, hence the same outcome MSE 0.22390.2239. Their conditional targets qg​(P)=𝔼​[g∣P]q_{g}(P)=\mathbb{E}[g\mid P] are respectively SS, S+0.08S+0.08, and SS. These targets are already nondecreasing. Thus the population PAIC excess risks are 00, 0.00640.0064, and 00: the two hidden-state errors average away at each score, whereas the constant offset remains.

Frozen finite-sample procedure.

For each calibration count C∈{20,50,100,500,2000}C\in\{20,50,100,500,2000\}, we generate 2,000 independent samples. Each sample is a multinomial count vector over the four equiprobable states, shared by all three probes. Different values of CC use independent samples. A separate 50-repetition pilot uses distinct random streams and does not tune this design. We fit weighted isotonic regression at P∈{0.37,0.67}P\in\{0.37,0.67\}. If both scores occur, their mean probe targets are retained unless they cross, in which case they are pooled using the observed counts. If one score is absent, both fitted values equal the observed group’s mean target. This extension rule is fixed before sampling. Integer cross-products of the targets, expressed in hundredths, distinguish strict crossings from exact ties.

For a fitted map ff, all expectations below are over the known population, conditional on its calibration sample. With b∈{0,0.08,0}b\in\{0,0.08,0\} for the three probes, we calculate

L(f)−(N+I)=𝔼[(f(P)−S)2],u=𝔼[(f(P)−(S+b))2],L⁡(f)−(N+I)≤(|b|+u)2.\begin{gathered}L(f)-(N+I)=\mathbb{E}[(f(P)-S)^{2}],\qquad u=\mathbb{E}[(f(P)-(S+b))^{2}],\\ L(f)-(N+I)\leq(|b|+\sqrt{u})^{2}.\end{gathered}

Here uu is the population probe-loss gap above its monotone minimum, not empirical fitting loss. Exact evaluation removes outcome-sampling noise; the reported Monte Carlo uncertainty comes only from calibration samples.

Results and scope.

Table 3 separates fitting variation from the persistent offset bias. At C=2000C=2000, mean excess risks are approximately 3.90×10−73.90\times 10^{-7}, 0.00640110.0064011, and 3.16×10−53.16\times 10^{-5}. Equal probe MSE does not imply equal finite-sample variation: the within-score target amplitudes are 0.020.02, 0.100.10, and 0.180.18. More calibration samples bring the offset probe’s repair toward its biased population target, not toward the scalar optimum.

All 30,000 fitted maps satisfy the bound to numerical tolerance 10−1210^{-12}. For the two zero-offset probes, the bound is an algebraic equality. Appendix B.5 examines the same mechanism in learned probes.

B.3 Raw-score repair under distribution shift

The shift study crosses two models, three shifts, three refits, source fitting budgets F∈{100,500,1000}F\in\{100,500,1000\} and unlabeled adaptation budgets U∈{100,500,1000}U\in\{100,500,1000\}. Difficulty transfer uses MATH levels 1–2 as source and level 3 as target; task transfer uses GSM8K as source and MATH as target; subject transfer uses 10K general knowledge and history as source and science as target, excluding mathematics. Test sets have 598, 3,085 and 1,300 prompts per refit. The primary comparison fixes F=U=500F=U=500.

Platt and beta minimize outcome-targeted cross-entropy, with soft targets for grades; beta uses sigmoid⁡(a​log⁡P−b​log⁡(1−P)+c)\operatorname{sigmoid}(a\log P-b\log(1-P)+c) with nonnegative bounded a,ba,b (Kull et al., 2017). The flexible scalar model uses 60 histogram-boosting iterations, eight leaves, minimum leaf size 32 and unit L2L_{2} regularization. Ridge uses penalty 10; the tree probe, prespecified as primary, uses 48 ExtraTrees with maximum depth 10, minimum leaf size 32 and feature fraction .7. The group method fits an at-most-eight-leaf feature tree on one source half and within-leaf isotonic maps on the other, following Chen et al. (2024) with projected answer states instead of their query embeddings. Scalar methods and PAIC serve only PP; direct probes need the 72 probe inputs. The target-isotonic diagnostic uses labeled target prompts and no source labels, so it is a yardstick rather than an equally supervised competitor.

With either probe, PAIC has lower mean risk than every source-fitted scalar map and the unchanged score in all six cells (Table 4). Tree PAIC improves on source-fitted beta in all 18 refits, with all 18 pointwise paired intervals below zero; ridge PAIC does so in 17. Against the flexible scalar map, Qwen subject transfer is less decisive: one of three ridge intervals and two of three tree intervals exclude zero. Relative to source label-isotonic, tree and ridge PAIC lower mean risk by 4.94.9–16.4%16.4\% and 1.41.4–16.2%16.2\% and close 6262–102%102\% and 1717–102%102\% of the gap to the target-isotonic yardstick (median 87%87\% over both probes and six cells). Direct probes have lower mean risk in all six cells. PAIC improves the deployed map of P; retaining the probe inputs enables further risk reduction. The group calibrator, the closest published comparator, improves on source label-isotonic in four of six cells but is above PAIC in all six and above the unchanged score under Qwen task transfer.

Learning curves and boundaries.

With U=500U=500, increasing FF from 100 to 1,000 lowers difficulty-shift ridge-PAIC risk from .241287 to .237034 for Llama and from .194314 to .193718 for Qwen. Under Llama task transfer, ridge PAIC worsens from .234934 at F=500F=500 to .249177 at F=1000F=1000, above the unchanged score (.247051), while tree PAIC stays stable (.218722 to .218441); probe and variant choice is therefore left to the labeled adoption test of Appendix B.10. More unlabeled target data changes risk less: Qwen task-transfer ridge risks are .165542/.166735/.166094 at U=100/500/1000U=100/500/1000. Within a single domain, at F=U=500F=U=500, ridge PAIC and label-isotonic differ by less than .0004 in every GSM8K, MATH and 10K cell mean, as expected when source and target share one score–correctness curve. On the archived learned score, every scalar map changes risk by less than 10−310^{-3} (Table 5); PAIC improves on label-isotonic by .000108–.000401 in the four full-budget means.

B.4 Equally informed adaptation

Design.

The comparison reuses the six model–shift settings and three overlapping refits above. Every adaptation method is allowed 500 labeled source prompts, 500 unlabeled target prompts and an independent pool of 500 source prompts whose labels are masked; each prompt keeps its eight siblings with equal weight. The tree and ridge teachers are reused; trees are primary and ridge is a prespecified sensitivity. Target-probe Platt and beta fit exactly the target prompts and teacher predictions used by PAIC, minimizing soft cross-entropy. Source-distilled isotonic fits the same teacher’s predictions on the masked source pool, isolating the value of target adaptation. Importance-weighted (IW) isotonic fits the 500 source outcomes with prompt-level density ratios estimated by five-fold domain classification (Park et al., 2020); the classifier receives the prompt means of the 72 probe inputs and the mean original confidence, but no outcomes or task labels. Logistic regularization is fixed at C=0.1C=0.1, odds are clipped to [0.1,10][0.1,10], and one weight applies to all siblings of a prompt. The group calibrator uses no unlabeled target prompts and serves group features, so its risks appear in Table 4.

Paired contrasts.

The 72 prespecified primary contrasts compare tree-PAIC with the four comparators in each of the 18 panels. Losses average siblings within a prompt, and uncertainty uses 1,999 prompt bootstraps with pointwise intervals and approximate normal-Bonferroni intervals across all 72 contrasts (Table 7, Figure 5). Within-panel four-contrast max-tt intervals favor PAIC in 53 of 72 contrasts and importance weighting in one; no contrast favors a comparator under the global adjustment. PAIC’s estimate is higher in five contrasts: against beta by .000046 (Qwen task) and .000316 (Llama difficulty), and against IW by .003894 and .001453 (Llama difficulty) and .000373 (Qwen difficulty), each in one refit. Only the .003894 difference has a pointwise interval excluding zero, [.001080,.006801][.001080,.006801]. Direct tree predictors remain more accurate than PAIC in all six settings.

Fitting objective.

The cross-entropy maps and isotonic PAIC minimize different objectives. A sensitivity analysis fits 36 further Platt and beta maps that minimize squared error to the same target teacher values, with the same 10−610^{-6} parameter penalty and bounds and two fixed starts chosen by adaptation loss alone. Every selected map lowers adaptation teacher error relative to its cross-entropy version, and on test data squared-loss beta improves on cross-entropy beta in 15 of 18 refits (Platt in 14). PAIC still has the lower estimate against squared-loss Platt in 18 of 18 refits and against squared-loss beta in 15 of 18, with mean gains over the latter of .000125–.001368 per cell. The objective thus explains part of the gap to parametric maps; the remainder is a modest mapping benefit that holds in most refits.

Overlap and importance weighting.

Natural-shift overlap differs sharply (Table 8). Clipping inflates the effective sample size (ESS) by equalizing tiny weights but does not restore missing support. Task and subject shifts have nearly separable source and target inputs. We therefore also evaluate randomized GSM8K shifts with known overlap. Estimated and oracle importance weighting give similar risks in these controls, and all target-aware maps have similar mean risks (Table 8). Six randomized GSM8K controls therefore assign each prompt to source or target with known probability e⁡(X)=0.2+0.6​sigmoid⁡(z)e(X)=0.2+0.6\,\operatorname{sigmoid}(z), where zz standardizes the prompt’s mean original confidence; this provides overlap and preserves the conditional outcome law by design. In these controls all target-aware maps nearly tie, PAIC has the lowest mean risk, and estimated and oracle (e/(1−e)e/(1-e)) weighting agree.

B.5 Conditional bias of learned probes

The raw-score diagnostic compares ridge probes with 16 or 72 inputs and ExtraTrees, fitted on identical source labels. Bounded perturbations separate score-dependent bias from cancelling error: independent-sign perturbations raise probe MSE by .006470 on average but PAIC risk by only .000029, whereas score-dependent perturbations raise MSE by .000459 and PAIC risk by .001161.

On the archived learned score, four probes (ridge penalties .1 and 10; 32 shallow and 64 deeper ExtraTrees) and nested unlabeled calibration prefixes give 720 probe fits and 2,880 maps. Reversals persist: on GSM8K Qwen (seed 42, fold 0, quarter budget), shallow trees have lower direct risk than ridge (.090788 versus .094128) but a worse PAIC map (.089870 versus .087777; paired interval for the gap [.000632,.003630][.000632,.003630]).F Coarse bins approximate, rather than identify, the conditional-bias norm of Theorem 3.2: the reversals support the mechanism, while reliable target-label-free probe selection remains open, and the labeled adoption test is the safeguard.

B.6 A learned score transferred to harder MATH problems

This study uses a learned scorer rather than the raw likelihood score. Each model’s final scorer, trained on GSM8K, is applied to cached MATH answers with eight answers per problem (Hendrycks et al., 2021); levels 1–2 supply 3,110 source problems and level 3 supplies the target. Difficulty is observational: the levels also differ in subject mix and answer length. Labels are the original parser matches, replayed exactly for all 91,66491{,}664 answers. A fixed hash splits the source problems into probe fitting FF (1,555), scalar-map calibration CC (777) and source evaluation (778). The probe takes the scorer’s 32 learned coordinates and PP (a 256-component Nyström ridge model). Label-isotonic is fitted on FF outcomes and source PAIC on CC with the probe’s predictions, so both use the same 12,440 source labels; the direct probe serves the richer inputs.

Transfer.

Both scalar repairs lower squared loss relative to PP on source and on target, and all eight corresponding Bonferroni-adjusted (99.6875%99.6875\%) intervals exclude zero. On source, the PAIC–isotonic difference is unresolved; on all 2,619 level-3 problems, label-isotonic is lower by 0.000870.00087 for Llama and 0.000940.00094 for Qwen, both intervals excluding zero. The repairs’ gain over PP shrinks from source to target for Llama (0.093910.09391 to 0.057930.05793 for PAIC) and grows for Qwen (0.004660.00466 to 0.012420.01242).

Adaptation with unlabeled target answers.

Keeping the scorer and probe fixed, target PAIC refits only the monotone map, on 777 level-3 problems whose labels are not used; the remaining 1,842 level-3 problems form a common evaluation set (Table 9). For Llama, target PAIC lowers risk by 0.006330.00633 relative to source PAIC and by 0.005520.00552 relative to source label-isotonic (Bonferroni 98.75%98.75\% intervals [−0.00792,−0.00479][-0.00792,-0.00479] and [−0.00689,−0.00418][-0.00689,-0.00418]). The gain is not uniform across subjects: Prealgebra risk rises by 0.004560.00456 (pointwise interval [0.00194,0.00715][0.00194,0.00715]), while Intermediate Algebra and Precalculus improve most. For Qwen, the change relative to source PAIC is unresolved (−0.00008-0.00008, interval [−0.00026,0.00010][-0.00026,0.00010]), and target PAIC remains 0.000830.00083 above source label-isotonic ([0.00019,0.00149][0.00019,0.00149]). In the highest score bin, the fixed probe overpredicts correctness by 0.0680.068 for Llama and 0.0490.049 for Qwen; such coarse bins are consistent with score-conditional bias but neither estimate bnb_{n} nor isolate the cause of any risk difference.

Review decisions.

With perfect review at cost c=0.10c=0.10 (accept when the score is at least 0.900.90), both target PAIC maps review every answer and so match the always-review loss 0.100.10. For Qwen, acceptance falls from 73.00%73.00\% under source PAIC to zero because the largest adapted score, 0.8995160.899516, lies just below the threshold, whereas source PAIC reaches 0.9000150.900015. A small change in squared risk near a threshold can thus change many decisions.

B.7 Controlled presentation changes

This study asks whether an unlabeled target projection improves a scalar confidence when a problem’s presentation changes but its answer and label do not. Constructed problems track integer counts of red tokens through additions, removals and transfers among crates. Eight strata cross 4/8/12/16 operations with 4/6 crates, and each structural family has two numerical instances. Entity renaming, fact reordering and irrelevant context supply three known transformations. Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct each answer the canonical problem once, and every presentation reuses that answer, so only the confidence changes. The design tests held-out structural families under known transformations.

Score, teachers and supervision.

Here PP is the model’s probability of the Yes verification sequence, normalized over Yes and No for the question and fixed answer; it differs from both the answer-token likelihood and the fixed-choice score of Appendix C. The rich teacher uses three prefix hidden-state blocks (last, middle and quarter) plus PP; its matched score-only teacher uses PP alone. Both are Nyström kernel ridge models with 256 components, ridge penalty 1 and unit kernel scale, fitted with five family folds. Per model, the family-disjoint roles are fitting FF (1,200 families; 2,400 graded answers), canonical projection CC (600 families), target projection UU (600 families, one transformed view each, balanced within strata), and evaluation TT (1,800 families; 3,600 graded answers). Canonical fitting uses the 2,400 labeled rows. Augmented fitting, denoted aug\mathrm{aug}, uses the three transformed views of the same answers: 7,200 rows with the same 2,400 labels. Thus ISOaug\mathrm{ISO}_{\mathrm{aug}} fits label-isotonic to transformed scores; target PAIC projects the canonical rich teacher on UU; PAICaug\mathrm{PAIC}_{\mathrm{aug}} projects a transformed-trained rich teacher; and PAICP,aug\mathrm{PAIC}_{P,\mathrm{aug}} projects its score-only counterpart. Source PAIC projects on canonical CC.

Evaluation.

Every evaluation answer has a binary solver-based grade; answers that cannot be parsed count as incorrect (49 of 3,600 for Llama, including 37 truncated, and 16 for Qwen, including 10 truncated). Primary risk averages the two instances and three transformed presentations within each family and applies fixed stratum weights: 0.050.05 for each four-operation stratum and 0.150.15 for each other stratum. Families, not presentation rows, are the sampling units. The six primary contrasts in Figure 3 use approximate stratified finite-population Welch-tt intervals with α=0.05/6\alpha=0.05/6 each, conditional on the fits and grades. All six point estimates favor the comparator; four intervals exclude zero and the two Qwen augmented comparisons are unresolved (Table 10). In point estimates, transformed-view fitting helps the direct rich teacher most, while no projected map recovers that gain.

B.8 An offline verifier as teacher

Can a score-only map keep part of the benefit of an extra verifier pass? For Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct under the MATH difficulty shift, a fixed hash selects one cached answer per prompt: 500 labeled level-1/2 source prompts, 500 unlabeled level-3 adaptation prompts and 598 level-3 test prompts. A second pass of the same checkpoint scores True against False for the question and fixed answer, without a reference answer. A positive Platt map fitted to the 500 source grades calibrates this verifier, and the calibrated verifier is the teacher. PAIC fits a nondecreasing map of the likelihood score to the teacher on the adaptation prompts. Target Platt and monotone beta maps receive the same inputs and teacher values, fitted by cross-entropy (CE) or Brier loss; source isotonic and Platt use the source grades. Supervision is thus shared, while the information and computation needed at serving differ.

PAIC lowers squared risk from 0.212740.21274 to 0.197180.19718 while serving only the original score, and it improves on both target Platt variants (Table 11). Comparisons with source isotonic, source Platt, the raw verifier and both target beta variants are unresolved. The calibrated verifier reaches 0.155060.15506: the projection keeps part of the teacher’s benefit and leaves a gap of 0.042120.04212 ([0.02548,0.05914][0.02548,0.05914]).

Review decisions and cost.

Under the perfect-review policy, PAIC accepts only 6 of 598 answers at c=0.10c=0.10 (loss 0.104010.10401, just above reviewing everything), and all four target Platt/beta variants review every answer; at c=0.25c=0.25 and 0.500.50 the calibrated verifier has the lowest loss (Table 12). On a separate sample of 16 newly generated answers, the extra verifier pass took 0.04010.0401 seconds against 11.20311.203 seconds for generation and original confidence, about 0.36%0.36\% of the recorded time. The separate timing experiment measures the verifier’s incremental inference cost for this fixed teacher.

B.9 Controlled tests of residual-corrected comparisons

These known-population controls evaluate the comparison procedure of Appendix A.6; they contain no fitted repairs or LLM predictions. Independent prompts have uniformly distributed (S,H)∈{0.35,0.65}×{−1,1}(S,H)\in\{0.35,0.65\}\times\{-1,1\}, conditional mean m=S+d​Hm=S+dH and starting score P=S+cP=S+c, with d=0.1d=0.1 and c=0.02c=0.02 by default. The six candidates are PP, SS, S+0.1​HS+0.1H, 1/21/2, S−0.1​HS-0.1H and gg, and the probe is one of mm, m+0.08m+0.08, SS or 1−m1-m. The 28 settings comprise 12 singleton binary controls (four probes, JL∈{100,500,2000}J_{L}\in\{100,500,2000\}, JU=4​JLJ_{U}=4J_{L}), four balanced-pool controls (JL=JU=500J_{L}=J_{U}=500), four no-useful-repair controls (d=c=0d=c=0), six sibling controls (K=8K=8 with ρ∈{0,0.8}\rho\in\{0,0.8\}, or K=2K=2 versus 1616 by subgroup) and two graded controls; each has 2,000 repetitions. We compare paired labels, the uncorrected proxy comparison and correction with λ=1\lambda=1, using the global empirical-Bernstein ranges over the 15 pairs at α=0.05\alpha=0.05.

Correction removes proxy bias.

Outside the no-useful-repair controls, the true contrast is L⁡(P)−L⁡(S)=0.0004L(P)-L(S)=0.0004, favoring SS. For the offset binary control with (JL,JU)=(500,2000)(J_{L},J_{U})=(500,2000), mean estimates over 2,000 repetitions are 0.0004125840.000412584 for paired labels, −0.002805102-0.002805102 for the proxy and 0.0003970340.000397034 after correction (Monte Carlo standard errors 0.0000190790.000019079, 0.0000020000.000002000 and 0.0000187620.000018762): the proxy precisely estimates the wrong target, −0.0028-0.0028. Corrected-to-labeled estimator SD ratios are 0.98010.9801, 1.00001.0000 and 1.30441.3044 for the binary oracle, blind and reversed probes and 0.79790.7979 for the graded oracle, so precision gains depend on the probe.

Two-sided bounds cover but do not decide.

Both empirical-Bernstein procedures have 100%100\% observed simultaneous coverage and retain PP in every repetition. At (JL,JU)=(2000,8000)(J_{L},J_{U})=(2000,8000) the range-only half-widths are about 0.016550.01655 for paired labels and 0.040880.04088 for correction, exceeding the largest true improvement, 0.01040.0104. A normal benchmark with Bonferroni critical values has observed simultaneous coverage 0.9710.971–0.9910.991 for paired labels and 0.97250.9725–0.9910.991 for correction across the 28 settings, with asymptotic justification only. This motivates the one-sided adoption test of Proposition 3.3.

B.10 Adoption tests with matched finite inference

Procedures.

For non-original candidate hh and prompt jj, Dj​hD_{jh} is the prompt-averaged squared-loss difference from PP. A certificate δh≥sup|h−P|\delta_{h}\geq\sup|h-P| gives the range [−Bh,Bh][-B_{h},B_{h}] with Bh=δh​(2−δh)B_{h}=\delta_{h}(2-\delta_{h}); observed maxima are not certificates. For a scalar map, supp|τ^​(p)−p|\sup_{p}|\hat{\tau}(p)-p| is computed exactly from the fitted map, while a feature-based candidate that admits no tighter bound takes the certificate implied by its output range, which widens BhB_{h}. Both primary tests use the one-sided null that hh does not lower expected squared loss, the same certified ranges, the same family of HH candidates, the same fixed comparison budget and familywise α=0.05\alpha=0.05. The one-sided empirical-Bernstein (EB) test (Maurer and Pontil, 2009) certifies hh when

D¯h+2​sh2​log⁡(2​H/α)n+7​(2​Bh)​log⁡(2​H/α)3​(n−1)<0,\overline{D}_{h}+\sqrt{\frac{2s_{h}^{2}\log(2H/\alpha)}{n}}+\frac{7(2B_{h})\log(2H/\alpha)}{3(n-1)}<0,

and betting certifies hh when the e-value of Proposition A.14, with 𝒮={.05,.1,.25,.5,.9}\mathcal{S}=\{.05,.1,.25,.5,.9\}, reaches H/αH/\alpha. Both adopt the certified candidate with the lowest paired mean and otherwise retain PP. Assisted variants add a frozen probe’s contrasts on independent unlabeled prompts (Appendix A.7), with the weight grid {0,.25,.5,.75,1}\{0,.25,.5,.75,1\} and candidate-by-weight Bonferroni correction. Two-sided EB intervals, which use log⁡(4​H/α)\log(4H/\alpha), and same-sample PPI++ (Angelopoulos et al., 2024), with weights clipped to [0,1][0,1], serve as references; PPI++ is asymptotic. Guarantees apply to a prespecified budget and procedure, not to choices made after inspecting the sweeps.

Known-risk simulations.

The matrix crosses six finite-support populations (binary or graded null, constant gain and heterogeneous gain), oracle or reversed probes, n∈{25,50,100,250,500,1000,2000}n\in\{25,50,100,250,500,1000,2000\} labeled prompts, and r∈{0,1,4}r\in\{0,1,4\} unlabeled prompts per label. Each of the 252 cells has 2,000 datasets and the same five candidates. A prompt state is uniform over four conditional means μ=(.2,.4,.6,.8)\mu=(.2,.4,.6,.8) with z=(1,−1,1,−1)z=(1,-1,1,-1). The original score is P=μ+oP=\mu+o, where o=.04o=.04 under the null, .16.16 under constant gain, and (.02,.02,.18,.18)(.02,.02,.18,.18) under heterogeneous gain; the alternatives are μ−.04\mu-.04, μ+.04​z\mu+.04z, μ−.04​z\mu-.04z and μ+o+.005\mu+o+.005. Binary siblings are Bernoulli(μ\mu); graded siblings are μ±.04\mu\pm.04 with equal probability. With probability .8 all eight siblings share one draw. The null therefore has three risk-tied repairs and one harmful repair, and adopting a tie counts as a false improvement. Across 168,000 null decisions per method, paired betting certifies a tie 50 times and assisted betting 26 times; neither ever selects a harmful candidate, the largest cell rate is .2%.2\%, and the EB tests make no null certification. Asymptotic PPI++ made 3,120 false adoptions, 41 of them harmful (largest cell rate 3.25%3.25\%).

Matched to the same hypotheses, betting reaches the criterion with half the labels in three populations and a quarter in the fourth (Table 13, Figure 4). Paired betting and one-sided EB do not use the probe, so their crossings are the same for oracle and reversed probes and for every unlabeled ratio: across all 24 alternative settings, betting crosses at 250–1,000 labels and one-sided EB at 500–2,000. The two-sided intervals overstate the binary heterogeneous gap, since the matched one-sided EB test crosses at 2,000. Proxy assistance does not improve betting’s crossings; constant-gain oracle contrasts have no variation for a proxy to remove.

Cached LLM panels.

The replay uses all feasible allocations from 30 raw-score panels (16 shared candidates, including five PAIC maps, two of them controlled perturbations) and 180 archived-score panels (eight shared candidates), with learned or reversed auxiliary probes; candidates and allocations are unchanged and nothing is refitted. False adoption is classified by a separate test set (Table 14). At 250 comparison prompts, beneficial adoption is 16.81%16.81\% for one-sided EB versus 66.73%66.73\% for betting, and 37.82%37.82\% versus 79.28%79.28\% at 500; at least one PAIC map is certified in 14.40%14.40\% versus 50.10%50.10\% and 32.73%32.73\% versus 67.55%67.55\% of allocations. Feasible panels and unlabeled ratios differ with budget, so these pooled percentages are not a common-population learning curve. Richer direct predictors account for 99.29%99.29\% of betting’s adoptions. Counting the same 500 source fitting labels, 14 of 36 panel/ratio combinations in which both tests reach 80%80\% beneficial adoption show at least twofold fewer total labels for betting. On the archived learned score, all five procedures retain the original in all 117,000 learned-probe allocations per method: its comparison pools hold 25–100 labels per block, and its scalar-map gains are below 10−310^{-3}.

B.11 Controlled residual audits: what each test can detect

Opposite subgroup errors can cancel at each score level. We ask which audit features can detect these errors under dependent answers and unequal answer counts. Scores are fixed, subgroup information is observed, and conditional means are known. A rerun of all 3737 configurations reproduces every rejection count (Appendix B.12).

Population, controls and label budgets.

Each independent prompt draws base rate S∈{0.35,0.65}S\in\{0.35,0.65\} and subgroup H∈{−1,1}H\in\{-1,1\} independently and uniformly. Binary outcomes have conditional mean S+δ​HS+\delta H. The reported score is either s=Ss=S or the fixed invertible distortion s=f⁡(S)=sigmoid⁡(logit⁡(S)/0.7)s=f(S)=\operatorname{sigmoid}(\operatorname{logit}(S)/0.7). The 3030 core configurations cross both scores with δ∈{0,0.05,0.10,0.20,0.35}\delta\in\{0,0.05,0.10,0.20,0.35\} and J∈{100,500,2000}J\in\{100,500,2000\}, using one answer per prompt. With s=Ss=S, positive δ\delta introduces hidden subgroup error while preserving scalar calibration; with s=f⁡(S)s=f(S), δ=0\delta=0 introduces scalar error alone. Positive δ\delta and distortion combine both.

Seven additional configurations hold J=500J=500 and s=Ss=S. Four use K=8K=8 answers per prompt, ρ∈{0,0.8}\rho\in\{0,0.8\} and δ∈{0,0.10}\delta\in\{0,0.10\}. Here ρ\rho is the probability of one shared outcome for all answers to a prompt; otherwise outcomes are independent conditional on S,HS,H. Two configurations use the same mechanism with ρ=0.8\rho=0.8, δ∈{0,0.10}\delta\in\{0,0.10\}, and K=2K=2 for H=−1H=-1 versus K=16K=16 for H=1H=1. The final, calibrated graded control uses K=8K=8, ρ=0.8\rho=0.8 and Y=S+σ⁡(H)​ϵY=S+\sigma(H)\epsilon, where ϵ\epsilon is a fair sign, σ⁡(−1)=0.05\sigma(-1)=0.05 and σ⁡(1)=0.15\sigma(1)=0.15. Its values already lie in [0.2,0.8][0.2,0.8], so the implementation’s clipping leaves the declared mean unchanged. The shared-outcome mechanism also applies to this control.

All methods receive the same JJ labeled audit prompts. In each repetition, the learned auditor also uses 500500 independent, single-answer training prompts from the same outcome model. It fits residuals Y−sY-s by ridge regression on the four joint-state indicators, with summed squared loss, penalty 11 and no intercept. Its predictions h⁡(S,H)h(S,H) are clipped to [−1,1][-1,1] and frozen before auditing. These additional training labels are counted separately.

A common statistic, four different null hypotheses.

Each test asks whether mean residuals align with its features, defining its own null (Table 15). The one-hot vectors e(S,H)e_{(S,H)} and eSe_{S} indicate joint-state and score membership. All kernels use k⁡(z,z′)=⟨Φ⁡(z),Φ⁡(z′)⟩k(z,z^{\prime})=\langle\Phi(z),\Phi(z^{\prime})\rangle, without a bandwidth search. The feature, subgroup and learned tests observe S,HS,H directly, without learning subgroup representations from LLM outputs.

For every map, the residual contribution first averages within a prompt:

aj=1Kj​∑i=1Kj(Yj​i−sj​i)​Φ​(Zj​i),UJ=‖∑jaj‖2−∑j‖aj‖2J⁡(J−1).a_{j}=\frac{1}{K_{j}}\sum_{i=1}^{K_{j}}(Y_{ji}-s_{ji})\Phi(Z_{ji}),\qquad U_{J}=\frac{\|\sum_{j}a_{j}\|^{2}-\sum_{j}\|a_{j}\|^{2}}{J(J-1)}.

This weights prompts equally even when KK depends on HH and excludes all within-prompt pairs. The observed UJU_{J} is uncentered and may be negative. For calibration, xj=aj−a¯x_{j}=a_{j}-\bar{a} and independent Gaussian prompt multipliers give

Tb∗=‖∑jeb​j​xj‖2−∑jeb​j2​‖xj‖2J−1,p=1+∑b=11999𝟏{Tb∗≥JUJ}2000.T_{b}^{*}=\frac{\|\sum_{j}e_{bj}x_{j}\|^{2}-\sum_{j}e_{bj}^{2}\|x_{j}\|^{2}}{J-1},\qquad p=\frac{1+\sum_{b=1}^{1999}\mathbf{1}\{T_{b}^{*}\geq JU_{J}\}}{2000}.

Methods share multiplier draws within each repetition; each rejects at p≤0.05p\leq 0.05. Theorems A.20 and A.22 establish the population target and asymptotic justification. With fixed JJ and 1,9991{,}999 multiplier draws, finite-sample rejection rates remain an empirical question.

Each configuration has 2,0002{,}000 repetitions. A fixed master seed, with configuration and repetition indices, determines separate simulation and multiplier streams. Separate child streams generate audit and auditor-training data. Reported 95%95\% Wilson intervals describe each marginal Monte Carlo rejection rate. They are pointwise, not simultaneous intervals or paired intervals for method differences.

Results and interpretation.

Feature choice determines which residual moments are tested. Hidden subgroup errors cancel in the score-only moment; scalar-only errors cancel in the subgroup moment. Each satisfies the corresponding test’s null.

Across the seven fully calibrated configurations, feature-test rejection ranges from 0.04850.0485 to 0.05900.0590; each pointwise interval contains 0.050.05. This includes the stated sibling, unequal-KK and graded controls, without establishing validity outside them. The graded-null learned auditor rejects 126/2000=0.0630126/2000=0.0630 (pointwise Wilson interval [0.05317,0.07451][0.05317,0.07451]); with a new seed it rejects 4.70%4.70\% (Appendix B.12). Across the 4646 method-specific null cells, 4545 pointwise intervals contain 0.050.05; this count is neither a simultaneous validity statement nor an equivalence test.

Under hidden-only error at δ=0.05\delta=0.05, feature-test rejection increases from 0.12650.1265 to 0.44450.4445 to 0.97900.9790 as JJ increases from 100100 to 500500 to 2,0002{,}000. For scalar-only error at J=500J=500, the score-only test has higher observed rejection: 0.67700.6770, versus 0.55750.5575 for the feature test. These descriptive differences support choosing features for the errors of interest. Table 16 retains every configuration.

Checks and scope.

Deterministic fixtures check the cross-prompt formula and centered multiplier arithmetic against explicit pair sums. Audit-label budgets are JJ prompts per repetition; the auditor’s additional 500500 training labels are counted separately. These known-state simulations do not validate an LLM representation or a real-data repair, and non-rejection concerns the specified moment only.

B.12 Audit reruns and real-data audits

Reruns of the controlled audits.

Reruns of all 37 configurations of Appendix B.11 and nine diagnostics reproduce all 148 original rejection counts. The graded-null learned auditor rejects at 6.30%6.30\%; another seed gives 4.70%4.70\%, and the excess does not survive the declared Holm family. A binary 100-prompt Gaussian cell rejects 7.25%7.25\% and does survive that correction; replaying the identical observations against an exact conditional binomial reference gives 6.60%6.60\%, so that realization is rejection-rich even for a valid exact test. A 48-cell, 96,000-trial study varies sample size, outcome type, witness rank and multiplier count; at 100 prompts, binary Gaussian rates with 1,999 multipliers are 4.80/5.25%4.80/5.25\% across two seeds versus 4.25/4.30%4.25/4.30\% for the exact reference, and graded rates are 5.95/6.20%5.95/6.20\% versus 5.25/5.25%5.25/5.25\% for symmetric sign flips. No excess survives the 280-comparison Holm family, which is not a proof of uniform validity; exact or sign-flip references are the safer choice for small audits when the null permits.

A paired diagnostic of the graded-null cell.

We ran 18,000 further repetitions of the graded-null cell with 500 audit prompts, eight answers per prompt, sibling dependence ρ=.8\rho=.8 and 1,999 reference draws. Each repetition trains and freezes its witness before auditing. Three rejection indicators share the same outcomes: GLG_{L} uses the Gaussian procedure with residuals computed as in the controlled study (explicit outcome construction, averaging and score subtraction); GIG_{I} uses the Gaussian procedure with exact, sign-symmetric residuals; and SIS_{I} uses exact residuals with a sign-flip reference. The two Gaussian arms share multiplier draws. The prespecified contrasts are θG=𝔼⁡[GI−SI]\theta_{G}=\mathbb{E}[G_{I}-S_{I}] and θF=𝔼⁡[GL−GI]\theta_{F}=\mathbb{E}[G_{L}-G_{I}]. For each, we bound its two discordance probabilities separately and subtract the bounds; eight one-sided exact Clopper–Pearson tails at .00625.00625 give simultaneous coverage at least 95%95\% for both intervals.
