Audits of repaired LLM scores.

The raw-score audit fixes discovery-trained kernels, ridge witnesses, score bins and metadata groups before evaluating independent audit prompts. For ridge PAIC, approximate feature tests reject in 30 of 30 panels, score tests in 7 and metadata tests in 19; conservative bounded tests reject none. A partition audit adapts the local grouping-loss approach of Melo et al. (2026): discovery fits honest trees, optionally after spending its first 20%20\% on Platt calibration; debiased leaf energy subtracts within-leaf sampling variance; and only finite-rejecting leaves receive an audit-estimated residual offset, fixed before test evaluation. Across 300 raw-score plans, seven corrections in five panels trigger; all seven lower test point risk, by .02474–.05914, with favorable pointwise normal intervals, though none passes the conservative finite-sample certificate. On the archived learned score, 1,440 plans across 180 panels with 75–100 audit prompts each produce no finite rejection; non-rejection does not establish sufficiency.

A discovered family

All seven triggering leaves depend on answer length. One Qwen task-transfer leaf contains 510 test answers from 179 prompts, with mean raw confidence .91565, correctness .01176 and mean length 1,023.93 tokens. Inspecting raw states, all 20 sampled long answers hit the 1,024-token cap without an end-of-sequence token or closed boxed answer, whereas all 20 shorter siblings terminate with a closed box.

A mechanical screen.

The learned rule flags answers longer than 1,018 tokens; a mechanical rule flags exactly 1,024 tokens. The two groups nearly coincide (Table 17). On the 572-prompt, one-answer audit sample, the mechanical rule selects 32 prompts and the learned rule 33, with Platt-adjusted two-sided Hoeffding p=.01398p=.01398 and .01049.01049. Mechanical membership needs no labels; testing its residual bias uses 114 discovery labels for Platt calibration and 572 audit labels, and learning the tree uses 458 further discovery labels. The audit surfaced an unanticipated failure family; once found, a length rule describes it nearly exactly.

B.13 Decisions and incremental scoring cost

At prespecified review costs c∈{.05,.10,.20,.30,.40,.50}c\in\{.05,.10,.20,.30,.40,.50\}, accepting incurs 1−Y1-Y and reviewing incurs cc, assuming perfect review, and a value policy accepts at score 1−c1-c. A strictly monotone remap preserves ranking and isotonic pooling can add ties, so these experiments assess threshold choices and their transfer rather than risk–coverage curves. Baselines fit original-score thresholds directly on the same labels, fixed before test outcomes are evaluated. On the archived learned score, 21,600 policies over 180 settings give useful acceptance without a consistent advantage over directly fitted thresholds (Table 18). For GSM8K Qwen at c=.20c=.20, PAIC accepts 76.87%76.87\% with 5.10%5.10\% accepted error and loss .085398, versus .086033 for the directly fitted threshold; at c=.10c=.10 its loss .055525 exceeds that baseline’s .055109. At the full fitting budget, when both policies also use comparison labels, the comparison-fitted PAIC threshold has higher mean loss in 23 of 24 cell–cost settings than the original-score threshold fitted on FF plus comparison labels. At c=.05c=.05, Llama 10K PAIC accepts .56%.56\% of answers on average, with loss .050141, slightly worse than reviewing everything. Matching downstream label budgets matters: recalibration need not improve these decisions.

On cached inputs, with one thread, five warmups, twenty repetitions and randomized order, median batch-one latency is 14.5/8.7 microseconds for Llama/Qwen PAIC versus 263.1/142.6 for direct ridge and 3,616.0/1,863.9 for direct trees; at batch 256, PAIC takes .137/.113 microseconds per answer. These are incremental costs on cached inputs, excluding generation and state extraction.

Appendix C Fixed-choice confidence on BoolQ and ARC

Question and design.

The study asks whether hidden states help predict correctness beyond the full choice scores, and whether that information survives when deployment is restricted to a monotone function of one scalar score. Each model selects one option once per question, and every candidate predicts whether that fixed selection is correct. The design crosses four checkpoints, Llama 3.2 3B Instruct (Meta, 2024), Qwen 2.5 3B and 7B Instruct (Qwen Team, 2025) and Mistral 7B Instruct v0.3 (Mistral AI, 2024), with two benchmarks. The same questions occur across models, so the eight cells are not independent replications, and pretraining exposure to these public benchmarks is unknown.

Tasks and data separation.

BoolQ (Clark et al., 2019) supplies passage-based yes/no questions; its public validation split is the evaluation population TT, and its training data supply development DD, fitting FF and two unlabeled projection sets CC and UU from the same population. ARC (Clark et al., 2018) supplies a difficulty shift: Easy training supplies D/FD/F, Easy validation CC and Easy test a source evaluation set SS; Challenge training and validation supply unlabeled target inputs UU, and Challenge test is TT (Table 19). Groups of questions linked by normalized exact matches of questions, passages or IDs are kept within one role, and all predictions were saved before evaluation labels were joined.

Scores and candidates.

Each allowed option letter is one prefix-stable token with next-token logit ℓj\ell_{j}; the choice probabilities are qj=exp⁡(ℓj)/∑kexp⁡(ℓk)q_{j}=\exp(\ell_{j})/\sum_{k}\exp(\ell_{k}), the model selects the first maximizer j^\widehat{j}, and the scalar confidence is P=qj^P=q_{\widehat{j}}, conditional on the allowed choices. Every supervised candidate uses the same FF questions, and five label-blind folds that keep linked questions together select hyperparameters by out-of-fold Brier loss. The seven direct candidates are raw PP, label-isotonic, monotone Platt, a flexible PP-only predictor, ridge and tree predictors of the 24 choice-score features, and a rich ridge predictor that adds every coordinate of the middle and final hidden states. Six further candidates project three teachers (the selected scalar, score and rich predictors) onto nondecreasing functions of PP by isotonic regression on CC or UU, without their labels. Supervised labels are therefore matched, while PAIC additionally uses unlabeled inputs.

Primary comparisons.

At the full fitting budget on TT, each of the eight cells contributes four Brier-risk differences (first minus second; negative favors the first): rich direct minus the selected score predictor; rich-PAIC-UU minus the selected scalar predictor; rich-PAIC-UU minus score-PAIC-UU; and rich-PAIC-UU minus rich direct. All 32 effects form one family of approximate simultaneous 95%95\% intervals from 19,999 dependency-component bootstrap draws, conditional on the fits and fitting-based selections (Figure 2). Failure to resolve a difference does not establish equivalence.

Results.

Hidden states add resolved accuracy over the full choice scores in two of eight cells: rich ridge minus the selected score control is −0.00803-0.00803 for BoolQ Qwen3B (joint interval [−0.01243,−0.00362][-0.01243,-0.00362]) and −0.01131-0.01131 for BoolQ Mistral7B ([−0.01702,−0.00559][-0.01702,-0.00559]); the other six differences are unresolved. Rich-PAIC-UU versus the selected scalar control is unresolved in all eight cells (point differences negative in five), and so is rich-PAIC-UU versus score-PAIC-UU. Serving the rich predictor directly is more accurate than projecting it for each BoolQ model (differences 0.01210.0121–0.01690.0169) and for ARC Qwen3B (0.01010.0101); the other three ARC differences are unresolved. BoolQ’s projection sets share its fitting population, and ARC’s CC and UU differ in both population and size, so this design does not isolate the effect of adaptation.

Decisions.

For costs c∈{.05,.10,.20,.30,.50}c\in\{.05,.10,.20,.30,.50\}, a fixed rule accepts when s≥1−cs\geq 1-c and otherwise requests perfect review. On BoolQ, every candidate beats both reference policies at c=.20c=.20, but the pattern changes at other costs: at c=.50c=.50, rich-PAIC-UU equals the accept-all loss for Llama3B and Qwen7B and exceeds it for Qwen3B and Mistral7B. On ARC Mistral7B at c=.05c=.05, rich-PAIC-UU accepts nothing. The rich direct predictor has its own limits: on ARC Llama3B its decision loss exceeds that of the selected score-ridge control at every cost, although their Brier contrast is unresolved.

C.1 A larger checkpoint

We repeat the protocol for Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct, fitting the same 13 candidates at 25%, 50% and 100% of FF and forming a separate family of eight simultaneous intervals for the four questions on each benchmark. The selected full-score control is score trees on BoolQ and score ridge on ARC; isotonic is the selected scalar control on both. Six of eight intervals cross zero (Table 20): the richer direct predictor resolves no gain over the full-score control on either benchmark, and rich-PAIC-UU resolves no gain over the scalar control or score-PAIC-UU. The only resolved contrasts compare rich-PAIC-UU with its direct rich teacher, with opposite signs: projection increases risk on BoolQ and lowers it on ARC. The value of serving a richer teacher through one monotone scalar thus remains population-dependent at this scale; one checkpoint does not establish a trend with model size.

Appendix D Extended Related Work

Classical calibration and probabilistic prediction.

Calibration asks whether predictive probabilities agree with empirical outcome frequencies. Classical forecast decompositions separate reliability, resolution, and irreducible uncertainty (Murphy, 1973; DeGroot and Fienberg, 1983; Bröcker, 2009), while proper scoring rules provide decision-theoretic objectives for probabilistic prediction (Gneiting and Raftery, 2007). In machine learning, post-hoc methods such as Platt scaling, isotonic regression, temperature scaling, beta calibration, and Dirichlet calibration modify predictive probabilities without retraining the underlying model (Platt, 1999; Niculescu-Mizil and Caruana, 2005; Zadrozny and Elkan, 2002; Guo et al., 2017; Kull et al., 2017; Kull et al., 2019). Reliability diagrams and Expected Calibration Error (ECE) are widely used summaries, although their interpretation depends on binning and finite-sample estimation (Pakdaman Naeini et al., 2015; Vaicenavicius et al., 2019; Kumar et al., 2019; Roelofs et al., 2022). More recent studies also emphasize that calibration behavior depends on architecture, scale, pretraining, and distribution shift rather than following a universal relationship with accuracy (Minderer et al., 2021; Ovadia et al., 2019). Our analysis differs from work that asks only whether the reported scalar is calibrated: we ask which part of correctness risk remains recoverable after the prediction has already been compressed into that scalar.

Grouping loss, sufficiency, and feature-dependent calibration.

A scalar confidence score can be calibrated while hiding systematic differences among examples assigned the same value. Grouping loss formalizes the predictive information lost through this compression (Perez-Lebel et al., 2023); under squared loss, our information term I=𝔼⁡[Var⁡(m⋆​(Z)∣P)]I=\mathbb{E}[\Var(m^{\star}(Z)\mid P)] is precisely this quantity under the declared representation ZZ. Non-injective recalibration may further merge distinct score values and thereby increase grouping loss (Perez-Lebel et al., 2023). Related approaches enrich the conditioning information rather than repairing only the original scalar. Multiaccuracy corrects systematic residuals over identifiable subpopulations (Kim et al., 2018), while multicalibration requires calibration over many computationally identifiable groups (Hébert-Johnson et al., 2018). Semantic and representation-aware variants similarly use features to expose errors hidden by an aggregate score (Yang et al., 2023). Our decomposition separates this pre-existing information loss from an additional monotone-pooling term GG: even the population-optimal order-preserving repair can therefore be scalar-calibrated while remaining insufficient relative to ZZ.

Group-dependent calibration for LLMs.

Recent LLM work has begun to examine this distinction directly. Chen et al. (2024) use learned representation-based groups and fit label-supervised isotonic calibrators within those groups. Their deployed prediction therefore depends on both the original confidence and the learned group assignment. Melo et al. (2026) use grouping-loss estimates to identify local epistemic uncertainty and support auditing and deferral. These approaches exploit richer information at serving time. PAIC addresses a different constraint: richer features or a correctness model may be available during fitting, while deployment must retain a single map of the original score. Our theory therefore asks how much of a richer predictor can be transferred into that restricted interface, and which errors of the richer predictor affect the resulting scalar map.

Calibration under distribution shift.

Calibration commonly deteriorates when the deployment distribution differs from the calibration distribution (Ovadia et al., 2019; Minderer et al., 2021). Under covariate shift, importance weighting reweights labeled source observations to approximate target expectations (Shimodaira, 2000), and analogous ideas have been developed specifically for calibration (Park et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020). Under label shift, class priors can instead be estimated and corrected (Lipton et al., 2018; Alexandari et al., 2020). Other work uses unlabeled target data to estimate aggregate target performance, including ATC and difference-of-confidence approaches (Garg et al., 2022; Guillory et al., 2021). These methods primarily estimate target performance or reconstruct the target calibration objective through assumptions on distribution shift. PAIC takes an outcome-model route: a source-trained correctness probe predicts outcomes on unlabeled target examples, and these predictions define the target-population scalar repair. Accordingly, its relevant assumption is not an accurate target density ratio but small score-conditional probe bias on the target population.

Distillation and privileged information.

PAIC is also related to knowledge distillation, where a richer teacher provides soft supervision for a restricted student (Hinton et al., 2015), and to learning using privileged information, where additional features are available during training but unavailable at test time (Lopez-Paz et al., 2016). Standard distillation typically asks whether the student can approximate the teacher’s predictions or improve task accuracy. In our setting, the student hypothesis class is deliberately narrow: it is a nondecreasing function of a pre-existing scalar score. Consequently, global teacher accuracy is not the quantity governing transfer. Only the teacher’s systematic error after conditioning on the student input PP shifts the population projection. The PAIC guarantee makes this distinction explicit and shows why two probes with similar global prediction error can induce very different scalar repairs.

Selective prediction, abstention, and decision utility.

Confidence is often useful because it determines whether a model prediction is accepted, rejected, reviewed, or deferred. Selective classification studies this accuracy–coverage trade-off and constructs predictors that abstain on low-confidence inputs (Geifman and El-Yaniv, 2017); related reject-option and risk–coverage formulations likewise emphasize that uncertainty estimates are valuable through the decisions they support. These objectives are distinct from calibration itself: a monotone transformation can change probabilities while preserving ranking, whereas a fixed decision threshold can change behavior substantially after recalibration. Our decision experiments therefore evaluate prediction risk and downstream review utility separately rather than assuming that lower Brier risk implies a better selective policy. This distinction is particularly important when the application assigns explicit costs to acceptance and review.

Evidence for adopting a fitted repair.

A lower empirical loss on the data used to construct a repair is not evidence that the repair improves population risk. Prediction-powered inference (PPI) combines abundant model predictions with a smaller labeled sample by correcting the model-based estimate with observed residuals (Angelopoulos et al., 2023); PPI++ adapts the prediction contribution to improve statistical efficiency (Angelopoulos et al., 2024). We specialize this model-assisted estimation principle to paired squared-loss differences between frozen confidence candidates. The resulting identity also clarifies which component of probe error can reverse a candidate comparison. For finite candidate families, empirical-Bernstein inequalities provide observable simultaneous bounds (Maurer and Pontil, 2009). When the operational question is only whether a candidate improves over the deployed score, rather than estimation of every pairwise contrast, we additionally use bounded-mean betting (Waudby-Smith and Ramdas, 2024). Our contribution here is not a new generic inference paradigm, but an explicit separation between constructing a confidence repair and obtaining independent statistical evidence that it should be deployed.

Kernel calibration and residual-moment tests.

Kernel methods provide a complementary way to detect calibration errors that are invisible to low-dimensional summaries. MMCE (Kumar et al., 2018) and squared kernel calibration error (SKCE) (Widmann et al., 2019) embed calibration residuals in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, while distribution-matching formulations generalize these ideas to richer calibration conditions (Marx et al., 2023). In our setting the residual embedding

𝔼⁡[(Y−s⁡(Z))​Φ​(Z)]\mathbb{E}[(Y-s(Z))\Phi(Z)]

tests whether mean correctness errors remain associated with the declared features. With a sufficiently rich RKHS, a zero population embedding identifies the conditional mean predictor; with a finite feature map it tests only the corresponding residual moments. This feature dependence is intentional: an audit can only detect errors represented by its chosen features and kernel.

Dependence, clustered answers, and kernel inference.

Standard calibration estimators commonly treat evaluated examples as independent. LLM evaluation often violates this assumption because multiple answers are sampled from the same prompt and can share reasoning paths, difficulty, or failure modes. Pairing sibling residuals in a kernel U-statistic can therefore introduce a nonvanishing finite-sample term even when the population conditional-mean null holds. We instead treat prompts as the independent sampling units and average residual features within prompt before forming cross-prompt products. The corresponding multiplier procedure is related to wild-bootstrap methods for degenerate kernel statistics (Chwialkowski et al., 2014), but is formulated for the prompt-clustered statistic used here. This distinction is important for LLM settings with best-of-KK, self-consistency, repeated decoding, or other multiple-answer evaluation protocols.

Confidence estimation in language models.

LLM confidence can be derived from several fundamentally different signals. Token and sequence likelihoods use the model’s generative probability (Jiang et al., 2021); self-evaluation methods ask the model whether its own answer is correct, including P(True) (Kadavath et al., 2022); verbalized-confidence methods elicit numerical or linguistic uncertainty directly (Lin et al., 2022; Tian et al., 2023; Xiong et al., 2024); and sampling-based methods estimate uncertainty through agreement or disagreement among multiple generations (Wang et al., 2023; Kuhn et al., 2023; Farquhar et al., 2024). These quantities need not coincide: likelihood measures probability of the generated text, whereas answer-level confidence targets the probability that the realized answer is correct. Empirical studies consequently find that the quality of different confidence signals varies with model, task, elicitation method, and access regime. Our framework is agnostic to the origin of the base score: it treats any bounded scalar as the object to be retained, repaired, or compared against richer alternatives.

Semantic uncertainty and answer-level correctness.

Sampling-based semantic uncertainty methods address the fact that different surface forms can express the same underlying answer. Semantic entropy aggregates probability across meaning-equivalent generations (Kuhn et al., 2023; Farquhar et al., 2024), while self-consistency exploits agreement across reasoning trajectories (Wang et al., 2023). Nakkiran et al. (2026) study conditions under which calibration of semantic answer classes can emerge from local sequence-level loss optimality. These works concern uncertainty over semantic answers or distributions of generated responses. Our object is different: the answer AA has already been generated and fixed, and we ask whether a score attached to that realized answer predicts its correctness. Semantic or sampling-based signals can enter our framework as components of PP, as probe features in ZZ, or as richer candidate predictors, but the repair, comparison, and audit questions remain unchanged.

Internal representations and correctness probes.

A growing line of work predicts hallucination or correctness from hidden representations rather than from output probabilities alone (Orgad et al., 2025). Such probes can reveal correctness information that is absent from the reported scalar, making them natural witnesses of score insufficiency. They also create an important comparison problem: if hidden states are available at serving time, the direct probe should be compared against any scalar projection of that probe rather than being used only as a teacher. Conversely, when hidden states, additional sampling, execution checks, or verifier calls are available offline but unavailable or too costly at deployment, distilling their information into the existing scalar interface becomes meaningful. Our experiments therefore distinguish the information available for fitting from the information permitted at serving.

Relationship to our framework.

Taken together, prior work provides powerful tools for calibration, group-dependent correction, adaptation, model-assisted inference, and residual testing. Our framework connects these tools through a different organizing question: what evidence is required before changing a deployed confidence score? The risk decomposition first separates error recoverable from the scalar from information already lost by scalar compression; PAIC studies target-population repair when richer supervision is available only offline; labeled comparisons ask whether a fitted candidate actually improves correctness risk; and a separate prompt-level audit tests structured residual errors that average-risk comparisons can miss. Thus, “repair,” “adopt,” and “audit” are treated as distinct statistical problems rather than as different names for calibration.

Appendix E Broader Impact and Implications

Reliable confidence estimates matter when LLM outputs trigger review, abstention, regeneration or downstream actions. This work shows that improving average calibration is not sufficient: a scalar score may discard correctness-relevant distinctions, a fitted repair may not warrant adoption, and residual failures may remain after average risk improves. Separating these questions encourages deployment practices that state the information available to a confidence predictor, compare repairs on held-out correctness evidence, and audit structured residual errors at the right sampling unit. None of calibration, a successful repair or audit non-rejection is a certificate of safety: downstream utility depends on the application, decision costs, label quality and the failure modes an audit represents.

Where the distinctions change a decision.

For review or abstention, the question is whether the score separates the answers on which errors are costly. If relevant distinctions were discarded, moving a threshold or fitting another scalar map cannot recover them, and richer inputs become a candidate to evaluate; a repair that lowers average squared loss still needs comparison at the intended review cost. For a new population without labels, PAIC fits a score-only map from an available correctness probe, which helps when the probe’s inputs are available during adaptation but costly or unavailable at serving; its guarantee names the required transfer property—small probe bias averaged at each score—and held-out target labels are still needed for adoption. For regeneration or other corrective actions, an audit can locate feature-aligned mean errors, but whether a new answer fixes them needs its own comparison of success and cost.
